Module 5: Complications of the Neonate, Discharge Planning & Perinatal Loss

This module covers babies who need extra help in their first 28 days: preemies whose lungs and brains aren’t finished developing, babies who breathe in meconium, babies whose blood sugar drops or whose bilirubin climbs, babies withdrawing from substances, and babies with gut or brain bleeds. It ends with how nurses support families going home with a fragile baby and families whose baby has died.

🎯

Blueprint focus: neonatal physiology and assessment, high-risk newborn complications, family-centered care and grief support, discharge planning (apnea monitors and home oxygen), glucose infusion rate calculations, and medications such as indomethacin.

Lecture 1: Complications of the Neonate and Nursing Care

Slides 1–22 · Textbook Ch. 17 (Complications of the Neonate) · High-Risk Newborn Conditions chart · High-Risk Newborn Nursing Interventions
🍼5.1 Neonatal Complications: Definitions, Categories & Baseline AssessmentSlide 2 · Ch. 17

Neonatal complications are medical problems that show up in the first 28 days of life (the neonatal period). They can affect any organ system and are most often driven by three things: prematurity (organs aren’t finished), birth trauma, and infection. Early detection matters because catching a problem early lowers the chance of long-term illness (morbidity) or death (mortality). Care is multidisciplinary: nurses, pediatricians, neonatologists (newborn specialists), respiratory therapists, and others.

Categories of neonatal complications (slide 2)
CategoryExamples in this module
Respiratory distressRDS (respiratory distress syndrome), MAS (meconium aspiration syndrome), BPD (bronchopulmonary dysplasia), PPHN (persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn)
Feeding difficultiesPreterm suck-swallow-breathe immaturity, hypoglycemia, NAS (neonatal abstinence syndrome) poor feeding
Neurological issuesIVH (intraventricular hemorrhage), NAS, kernicterus from very high bilirubin
CardiovascularPDA (patent ductus arteriosus), congenital heart defects
GastrointestinalNEC (necrotizing enterocolitis)
InfectionsNeonatal sepsis, GBS (group B streptococcus)
Classifying newborns by gestational age and weight (Ch. 17)

The two strongest predictors of a baby’s health and survival are how many weeks of gestation the baby had and the birth weight. Gestational age is estimated with the Ballard score (a physical and neuromuscular exam). Prematurity and LBW (low birth weight) are the leading causes of infant death after birth defects.

📅 By gestational age
  • Preterm: born before 37 completed weeks
    • Extremely premature: under 28 weeks
    • Very premature: 28 to 31 6/7 weeks
    • Premature: 32 to 33 6/7 weeks
    • Late preterm: 34 to 36 6/7 weeks
  • Term: 37 to 41 6/7 weeks
  • Post-term: 42 weeks or more
⚖️ By weight
  • LBW: 1,500–2,500 g
  • VLBW (very low birth weight): 1,000–1,499 g
  • ELBW (extremely low birth weight): under 1,000 g
  • SGA (small for gestational age): below the 10th percentile for the baby’s age
  • LGA (large for gestational age): above the 90th percentile; macrosomia = 4,000 g or more
Normal newborn baseline (what “abnormal” is measured against)
FindingExpected rangeConcern
Respiratory rate30–60 breaths/minOver 60 = tachypnea (a sign of respiratory distress); pauses of 20 seconds or more = apnea
Heart rate110–160 beats/minOver 160 = tachycardia; under 100 = bradycardia
Axillary temperature36.5–37.5 °C (97.7–99.5 °F)Low = cold stress; temperature instability can mean infection
Blood glucoseAt or above about 45 mg/dL before routine feedsUnder 40–45 mg/dL = hypoglycemia
Newborn physiology: the transition at birth (supporting detail)

At birth the baby has to switch from the placenta to its own lungs within minutes. Understanding this switch explains many complications in this module:

Before birth (fetal)After birth (newborn)What goes wrong
Lungs are filled with fluid; the placenta does gas exchangeFirst breaths and labor squeeze out lung fluid; surfactant keeps alveoli openToo little surfactant = RDS; retained fluid = TTN; inhaled meconium = MAS
Lung blood vessels are tight, so blood skips the lungs through the ductus arteriosus and foramen ovaleOxygen relaxes lung vessels; the foramen ovale closes and the ductus closes within hours (up to 96 hours)Ductus stays open = PDA; lung vessels stay tight = PPHN
Glucose comes continuously from the parentBaby must use its own glycogen stores and feedingsLow stores or high insulin = hypoglycemia
The parent keeps the baby warmBaby makes heat by burning brown fat (it can’t shiver)Little fat or a cold room = cold stress (5.2)
The parent’s liver clears bilirubinThe baby’s immature liver must conjugate bilirubinBuildup = jaundice
📋 Neonatal nursing diagnoses and outcomes (Ch. 17)
  • Impaired gas exchange related to inadequate surfactant → outcome: RR 30–60 with no signs of distress
  • Risk for ineffective airway clearance related to meconium aspiration
  • Ineffective thermoregulation related to prematurity and little subcutaneous fat → temperature stays within normal limits
  • Imbalanced nutrition related to prematurity or hyperinsulinism → gains weight, adequate output, no hypoglycemia
  • Risk for infection → WBC normal, cultures negative
  • Pain related to procedures → decreased pain signs after interventions
  • Risk for injury (hypoxia, kernicterus, hypoglycemia, oxygen toxicity)
  • Risk for ineffective family coping, grieving, and risk for impaired attachment → parents visit, give care, ask for help
🫁 Classic signs of newborn respiratory distress (Ch. 17 Clinical Judgment)
  • Tachypnea: RR over 60
  • Expiratory grunting: the baby pushes air against a partly closed glottis to keep alveoli open
  • Nasal flaring
  • Retractions: skin pulling in at the sternum or between/under the ribs (intercostal, subcostal)
  • Duskiness or cyanosis (blue color)
Respiratory problems are the most common life-threatening conditions in newborns and the most common reason for NICU (neonatal intensive care unit) admission.
💡 Exam tip
Newborns can’t shiver to make heat (lecture). Cold stress, hypoglycemia, and respiratory distress feed one another, so thermoregulation is a priority in almost every neonatal question.
🌡️5.2 High-Risk Newborn Nursing Interventions: Temperature, Feeding, Breathing & Developmental CareInterventions doc · Ch. 17

These interventions apply to almost every high-risk baby, no matter the diagnosis. Think of them as the “foundation” you build every care plan on.

CategoryNursing interventionsWhy
Temperature
  • Minimize cold stress; keep skin temperature at 36.5–37.2 °C (97.7–99 °F)
  • Prevent rapid warming: set the warmer about 1–1.5 °C above the baby’s temperature; when the baby reaches it, raise it again until normal
  • Put a cap on the head (big source of heat loss)
Cold stress increases oxygen and glucose use, which leads to acidosis and hypoglycemia. Warming too fast can cause apnea and drops in blood pressure.
Foods and fluids
  • Monitor for hypoglycemia (under 40–45 mg/dL)
  • Assess tolerance of oral, breast, or tube feedings
  • Monitor hydration closely
  • Check gastric residual, bowel sounds, stool pattern, abdominal girth
  • Encourage EBM (expressed breast milk) or HDM (human donor milk) for preemies to lower NEC risk
  • Monitor weight gain or loss
Sick babies use energy fast and have small glucose stores. Belly changes can be the first clue to NEC.
Respiratory function
  • Position to improve oxygenation: semiprone or side-lying (teach parents that at home the baby must sleep on the back)
  • Keep the airway open; suction as needed
  • Stimulate or “remind” the baby to breathe (apnea)
  • Monitor O₂ therapy carefully: too much oxygen is harmful (ROP, BPD)
  • Assess effort: grunting, flaring, cyanosis, apnea
Prone/side-lying positions improve oxygenation in the monitored NICU setting only; back to sleep prevents SIDS (sudden infant death syndrome) at home.
Keeping a neutral thermal environment (NTE) (Ch. 17)

An NTE is the temperature range where the baby uses the least oxygen and calories to stay warm. Preemies lose heat easily because their skin is thin and they have little brown fat (the special fat newborns burn for heat). Nursing actions: dry the baby right away and remove wet linen, put on a hat, place babies under 32 weeks in a polyethylene plastic wrap to stop water and heat loss through the skin (TEWL, transepidermal water loss), use a chemical warming mattress (with a blanket between it and the skin), pre-warm anything that touches the baby, use the servo-control probe (taped on the skin, often midaxillary below the arm) on radiant warmers and incubators, use a double-walled incubator with humidity, and encourage kangaroo (skin-to-skin) care once stable. A baby can usually move to an open crib when medically stable and about 1,600 g or more.

How newborns lose heat (supporting detail)
MechanismWhat it meansPrevention
EvaporationHeat lost as moisture dries off wet skin (birth, baths)Dry the baby right away, remove wet linen, delay the bath, plastic wrap for babies under 32 weeks
ConductionHeat moves to a cold surface the baby touchesPrewarm scales, blankets, stethoscopes, mattresses; skin-to-skin
ConvectionHeat carried away by moving airKeep away from drafts, vents, and open doors; use incubator portholes; cap on the head
RadiationHeat moves to nearby cold objects not touching the baby (cold walls, windows)Keep cribs away from outside walls and windows; use a radiant warmer or double-walled incubator
🥶 The cold stress cascade
Newborns make heat by burning brown fat (nonshivering thermogenesis), which uses oxygen and glucose. A cold baby therefore develops increased oxygen use → hypoxia, hypoglycemia, metabolic acidosis, and in preemies, less surfactant production. Signs: cool skin, mottling, acrocyanosis, lethargy, jitteriness, poor feeding, respiratory distress.
Developmental care, pain, and skin (Ch. 17)
🌙 Developmental care
  • Quiet room, dim lights; cycle light for day/night after about 32 weeks
  • Cluster care for longer sleep, but don’t cluster several painful procedures together
  • Give the baby a break if stressed (color change, desaturation, splayed fingers)
  • Position in flexion, hands to midline, “nest” with blankets; reposition slowly every 2–3 hours
  • Kangaroo care: steadier temperature, less pain, more quiet sleep, better weight gain and bonding
🩹 Pain and skin
  • Use neonatal pain scales routinely
  • Oral sucrose and non-nutritive sucking (pacifier) for painful procedures; opioids for moderate-severe pain
  • Swaddling, holding, decreasing stimuli
  • Skin: Braden QD scale, use adhesives sparingly, no solvents, change position at least every 4 hours, hydrocolloid under devices
💡 Exam tip
When a question asks for the first action after birth, think warmth: dry the baby and place skin-to-skin (ATI example: “Place the newborn directly on the client’s chest” beats vitamin K, eye ointment, and the full assessment, because cold stress raises oxygen and glucose needs).
🐣5.3 Preterm Neonates: Risks, Assessment & Nursing CareSlides 4–5 · Ch. 17 · Chart

Preterm neonates are babies born before 37 weeks’ gestation. The earlier the birth, the less mature the lungs, brain, gut, immune system, and skin, and the more complications happen. Premature birth rates are highest among non-Hispanic Black mothers (13.8%), which reflects the social determinants you’ll study in Module 6.

Common complications (slide 4) and why they happen
ComplicationWhy preemies get it
RDSImmature lungs don’t make enough surfactant, so gas exchange is poor
Thermoregulation problemsLarge surface area for their body mass and little subcutaneous fat, so heat escapes fast
Feeding difficultiesPoor coordination of sucking, swallowing, and breathing until about 34 weeks; aspiration risk
InfectionImmature immune system, thin skin, many lines and tubes
Neurological complicationsIntracranial hemorrhage (IVH) and developmental delays
Also (Ch. 17)Apnea, hypotension, PDA murmur, anemia (frequent lab draws and low erythropoietin), hypoglycemia, jaundice, NEC, ROP
What a preemie looks like (Ch. 17 and High-Risk Conditions chart)
  • Low tone, extended posture (flexion increases with gestational age)
  • Thin, translucent, red or mottled skin; little fat; lanugo (fine body hair) between 20 and 28 weeks
  • Few or no plantar creases before 28–30 weeks; eyelids fused before 26–28 weeks; soft, folded ear cartilage before 34 weeks
  • Weak cry, diminished reflexes, tremors
  • Apnea: no breathing for 20 seconds or more, or shorter if the baby also has cyanosis, pallor, low tone, or bradycardia (HR under 100)
Nursing interventions (slide 4 plus Ch. 17)
✅ Slide priorities
  • Monitor respiration: continuous pulse oximetry; watch for apnea and distress
  • Maintain thermal regulation: incubator or radiant warmer for a neutral thermal environment
  • Feeding assistance: NG (nasogastric) or OG (orogastric) tube feedings when needed
  • Gentle handling, infection prevention, skin-to-skin and parent involvement (lecture)
🍼 Feeding details
  • Under 32 weeks: often need parenteral nutrition (IV nutrition, TPN) at first
  • Trophic feeds: tiny volumes that “wake up” the gut, not for calories
  • Before gavage feeds: check for distention, emesis, bloody stools, apnea
  • Pacifier during gavage (non-nutritive sucking)
  • Ready for oral feeds about 34 weeks: coordinated suck-swallow-breathe, gag reflex, hunger cues, quiet alert state
  • Human milk is preferred (lower NEC risk) but needs fortifier for extra calories, protein, minerals
  • Goal weight gain 15–20 g/kg/day; weigh daily, head and length weekly
🧬 Prevention before birth: antenatal steroids
Betamethasone or dexamethasone given to the pregnant person in preterm labor (when birth is expected within 7 days) speeds up fetal lung maturity. It is one of the most important interventions for preemies: it lowers RDS and IVH and death. Lung maturity can also be checked with the L/S ratio (lecithin/sphingomyelin: over 2:1 = mature; 3:1 in a diabetic pregnancy) or the presence of PG (phosphatidylglycerol) in amniotic fluid.
💡 Exam tip
Preemie priorities in order: breathing → warmth → glucose/feeding → infection prevention → family. Remember the AAP (American Academy of Pediatrics) car seat challenge before discharge for every baby born before 37 weeks (see 5.15).
🫁5.4 Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS) & SurfactantSlide 6 · Ch. 17 · Chart

RDS is the most common breathing problem in premature babies. It is caused by a lack of surfactant, a soapy substance (90% fat-based phospholipids) that coats the inside of the alveoli (tiny air sacs) and lowers surface tension so they don’t stick shut when the baby breathes out. The lungs start making surfactant at about 24–28 weeks and keep increasing to term. Without enough, alveoli collapse (atelectasis) with every breath, so the baby has to work harder and harder to reopen them.

What collapsed alveoli cause

Low oxygen (hypoxemia) and high CO₂ (hypercarbia) → respiratory acidosis (CO₂ can’t be blown off) and metabolic acidosis (cells make lactic acid without oxygen) → lung vessels constrict → blood bypasses the lungs through the ductus arteriosus and foramen ovale. Hypoxemia and acidosis further decrease surfactant production, so the problem feeds itself. Risk factors (chart): prematurity, maternal diabetes, and cesarean birth without labor (labor helps clear lung fluid and boost surfactant).

🚨 Signs and symptoms (slide 6)
  • Tachypnea: RR over 60
  • Nasal flaring and grunting
  • Intercostal or subcostal retractions, seesaw breathing
  • Cyanosis around the lips and extremities; gray or dusky skin
  • Begins at birth or within a few hours and gets progressively worse
  • Decreased breath sounds, crackles; lethargy, low tone
  • Chest x-ray: “ground glass” (reticulogranular) pattern with air bronchograms
✅ Nursing care (slide 6)
  • Surfactant through the ET (endotracheal) tube to improve lung compliance
  • Ventilation support: CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure) keeps alveoli open; mechanical or high-frequency ventilation if CPAP fails
  • Monitoring: ABGs (arterial blood gases), chest x-ray, blood culture if at risk for infection
  • Positioning: prone if not contraindicated, to improve ventilation
  • Keep an NTE: cold stress raises oxygen use and worsens acidosis
  • Daily weights and I&O (intake and output): dehydration thickens mucus; overhydration causes pulmonary edema; weight loss with more urine = expected diuretic phase of recovery
  • Minimize stimulation to lower oxygen demand
Surfactant replacement therapy (Ch. 17)
ItemDetails
TypesNatural (from calf, pig, or cow lung): beractant (Survanta), poractant alfa (Curosurf), calfactant (Infasurf). Synthetic: colfosceril (Exosurf).
ActionLowers alveolar surface tension so alveoli stay open, makes lungs easier to inflate, improves oxygenation
RouteInto the lungs through the ET tube (or a thin catheter or laryngeal mask to avoid intubation)
TimingProphylaxis: within 15 minutes of birth for babies under 27–30 weeks (especially without antenatal steroids). Rescue: within 6 hours for confirmed RDS needing more than 40% oxygen or a ventilator
Adverse effectsBradycardia, desaturation, tachycardia, reflux, gagging, cyanosis, ET tube blockage, hypotension. Don’t suction right after dosing unless the airway is blocked (it removes the drug).
BenefitsLess RDS, death, pneumothorax, IVH, and BPD

Complications of RDS: PDA, pneumothorax, BPD, pulmonary edema, hypotension, anemia, low urine output, hypoglycemia, ROP, IVH, seizures. Normal blood gas targets: PaO₂ 60–70 mm Hg (partial pressure of oxygen) and PaCO₂ 35–45 mm Hg.

💡 Exam tip
RDS = preemie + worsening grunting, flaring, retractions in the first hours. The cause is surfactant deficiency; the fix is surfactant + CPAP. The lecture also mentions a semi-upright (Fowler’s) position for comfort; the slide says prone if not contraindicated.
🫀5.5 Bronchopulmonary Dysplasia (BPD), Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA) & Retinopathy of Prematurity (ROP)Slide 20 · Ch. 17 · Chart

Slide 20 asks you to explore these textbook complications. All three are linked to prematurity and, for BPD and ROP, to the oxygen and ventilation used to save the baby.

Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD): chronic lung disease

BPD is lung scarring and inflammation in preemies who needed prolonged mechanical ventilation and oxygen. A baby still needing oxygen at 28 days of life is at risk. Fibrosis, collapsed areas, and over-stretched areas make the lungs stiff, and pulmonary edema develops.

🔍 Signs
  • Oxygen dependency, can’t wean off the ventilator
  • Retractions, wheezing, crackles (rales), rhonchi
  • Poor weight gain (breathing burns calories)
  • Fluid intolerance: edema, less urine, weight gain
  • Chest x-ray: sponge-like, cystic appearance
✅ Treatment = “support and time”
  • Minimize oxygen; wean slowly
  • Fluid restriction and diuretics (furosemide) for edema
  • Bronchodilators for bronchospasm; corticosteroids for inflammation
  • Extra calories (fortified milk/formula) because of fluid limits and work of breathing
  • Chest physiotherapy; RSV (respiratory syncytial virus) prophylaxis
  • Long-term: home oxygen, recurrent infections, CP (cerebral palsy), developmental delay
Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA)

Before birth, the ductus arteriosus connects the pulmonary artery to the aorta so blood skips the fluid-filled lungs. It normally closes within hours (up to 96 hours) after birth. In a PDA it stays open, so extra blood floods the lungs and the heart works harder. It occurs in about 45% of babies under 1,750 g and 80% under 1,200 g. Risk factors (chart): prematurity, RDS, birth asphyxia.

🩺 Assessment
  • Heart murmur at the upper left sternal border
  • Bounding pulses, wide pulse pressure (low diastolic BP)
  • Active precordium (you can see the heart beating)
  • Tachycardia, tachypnea, apnea, rising oxygen needs, trouble weaning
  • Signs of CHF (congestive heart failure)
  • Confirmed by echocardiogram
💊 Management
  • Fluid restriction (under 130 mL/kg/day) and diuretics
  • Indomethacin or ibuprofen (prostaglandin inhibitors) close the duct. The textbook notes they are used less today because of GI bleeding, decreased GFR (kidney filtration), and low urine output, so monitor urine output, kidney labs, and stools for blood
  • Surgical ligation (clip/suture) if medicine fails; baby is NPO (nothing by mouth) during treatment
  • Complications: CHF, chronic lung disease, kidney problems, NEC, IVH
Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP)

The blood vessels of the retina (the light-sensing back of the eye) aren’t finished growing in a preemie. Stress, especially high or fluctuating oxygen, interrupts normal growth, and then abnormal vessels sprout, bleed, and scar. Scar tissue can pull the retina off (detachment) and cause blindness. ROP is staged 1–5 (stage 4 = partial detachment, stage 5 = complete detachment). Up to 80% of babies under 1,000 g get some ROP, but about 90% recover with little or no vision loss.

  • Risk factors: prematurity and LBW, prolonged hyperoxia and ventilation, hypoxia, acidosis, sepsis, PDA, IVH, transfusions, steroid exposure, maternal diabetes/smoking
  • Screening: eye exam by a pediatric ophthalmologist at 4–6 weeks after birth for babies born under 30 weeks or under 1,500 g (and 1,500–2,000 g with complications)
  • Treatment: laser photocoagulation, cryotherapy, or vitreoretinal surgery
  • Nursing: keep SpO₂ (oxygen saturation) within the ordered range, use oxygen blenders and calibrated systems, careful oxygen during suctioning, dim lights and cover isolettes
  • Long-term: glaucoma, strabismus, cataracts, amblyopia, glasses
💡 Exam tip
“Too much oxygen can be a bad thing” (interventions doc): oxygen toxicity drives BPD (lungs) and ROP (eyes). PDA = murmur + bounding pulses; indomethacin = watch urine output and bleeding.
💚5.6 Meconium Aspiration Syndrome (MAS) & the Post-Term NeonateSlide 3 · Ch. 17 · Chart

Meconium is the baby’s first stool: thick, sticky, and tar-like. If the fetus is stressed in utero (usually hypoxia), the anal sphincter relaxes and meconium passes into the amniotic fluid (MSAF, meconium-stained amniotic fluid). Hypoxia also triggers deep gasping breaths, so the baby can inhale this fluid before, during, or right after birth. That is MAS.

What meconium does inside the lungs (lecture)
  • Airway obstruction of small and large airways (mechanical blockage)
  • Chemical pneumonitis: meconium irritates and inflames lung tissue
  • Surfactant inactivation: alveoli collapse
  • Air trapping and alveolar rupture → pneumothorax
  • Leads to PPHN (persistent pulmonary hypertension: lung vessels stay constricted after birth) and pneumonia
⚠️ Risk factors
  • Post-term infants (over 40–42 weeks): highest risk
  • Stressful deliveries / fetal distress: prolonged or difficult labor
  • Maternal hypertension, diabetes, infection
  • Low amniotic fluid (meconium is thicker and less diluted)
🔍 Signs
  • Green or yellow staining of fluid, skin, nails, and umbilical cord
  • Respiratory distress: tachypnea, cyanosis, grunting, retractions, flaring
  • Barrel-shaped, overdistended chest (air trapping)
  • Coarse crackles, rales, rhonchi, prolonged expiration
  • Low Apgar scores; limp, poor tone if significant
Nursing interventions (slide 3 and Ch. 17)
  • Suctioning: slide = immediate suctioning of the mouth then nose at delivery. Ch. 17 (current AAP neonatal resuscitation guidance): bulb-suction the mouth for a non-vigorous baby, avoid deep or vigorous suctioning; routine endotracheal (tracheal) suctioning is no longer recommended and is done only if thick meconium is blocking the airway. A clinician skilled in intubation must be present when MSAF is noted.
  • Oxygen therapy to keep saturations in range; ventilator support (conventional or high-frequency) if needed
  • Monitor for complications: pulmonary hypertension (PPHN), pneumonia, pneumothorax, hypoglycemia (breathing hard burns glucose), hypocalcemia, acidosis
  • Other therapies: surfactant, antibiotics for pneumonia, sedation on the ventilator, inhaled nitric oxide (iNO, relaxes lung vessels), therapeutic hypothermia (cooling) after asphyxia to protect the brain, ECMO (extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, a heart-lung bypass) if all else fails
Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN) (Ch. 17)

Normally the lung blood vessels relax after birth. In PPHN they stay constricted, so blood keeps bypassing the lungs through the ductus and foramen ovale (right-to-left shunting) and the baby stays hypoxic even on high oxygen. It affects 2–6 per 1,000 births, mostly term or near-term babies with hypoxia/asphyxia, MAS, RDS, sepsis, hypothermia, hypoglycemia, polycythemia, or diaphragmatic hernia. Late-pregnancy SSRI and NSAID use are maternal risk factors.

🔍 Signs
  • Cyanosis and low PaO₂ despite 100% oxygen
  • Symptoms within 12 hours of birth; tachypnea, retractions, grunting
  • Pre- vs. post-ductal SpO₂ difference of 5% or more (right hand higher than a foot)
  • Hypotension, murmur; echo shows high lung pressures
  • Hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia, metabolic acidosis
✅ Care
  • Goal: correct hypoxia and acidosis
  • Oxygen and ventilation (high-frequency if needed); inhaled nitric oxide relaxes lung vessels; surfactant; ECMO if all else fails
  • Dopamine to keep systemic pressure above lung pressure; sildenafil as a vasodilator; sedation and analgesia
  • Minimal handling, suctioning, and stimulation (these drop PaO₂)
  • Umbilical lines for labs and meds
  • Long-term: hearing loss, neurologic deficits, chronic lung disease
🧠 Birth asphyxia, HIE, and other CNS injuries (Ch. 17)
When oxygen to the brain is cut off before or during birth, the baby can develop HIE (hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy): low tone, poor feeding, seizures, and a decreased level of alertness. Therapeutic hypothermia (cooling the baby for a set period, started soon after birth) reduces brain injury and improves neurologic outcomes. Other birth-related CNS injuries include subgaleal hemorrhage (bleeding under the scalp, often after vacuum delivery; can cause severe blood loss and shock, so watch for a spreading, boggy scalp swelling, pallor, and rising heart rate) and intracranial bleeds. Nursing: neuro checks, seizure precautions, glucose and electrolytes, head circumference, and family support.
The post-term (postmature) neonate (Ch. 17 and chart)

A post-term pregnancy lasts 42 weeks or longer. The aging placenta can no longer deliver enough oxygen and nutrients (placental insufficiency), so the fetus burns its own fat and glycogen stores. Risks: MAS, fetal hypoxia (low fluid → cord compression), seizures from asphyxia, hypoglycemia (stores used up), hypothermia (fat lost), and polycythemia (hematocrit over 65%: the body makes extra RBCs to cope with low oxygen).

👀 What you see
  • Dry, cracked, peeling skin; no vernix
  • Long fingernails, profuse hair
  • Thin, wasted look; deep creases
  • Meconium staining
  • Poor feeding, hypoglycemia
✅ Nursing actions
  • Review history and Apgars; gestational age assessment
  • Watch respiratory status and SpO₂
  • Monitor glucose (jitteriness, poor feeding, apnea, lethargy)
  • Early and frequent feedings if breathing is stable
  • Check hematocrit (polycythemia); keep warm; I&O
  • Chart: “initiate delivery if compromised”
💡 Exam tip
MAS = post-term + green fluid + barrel chest + coarse crackles. After the airway, the next big watch items are PPHN, pneumothorax, and hypoglycemia.
⚖️5.7 Growth-Related Conditions: SGA/IUGR, LGA/Macrosomia & the Infant of a Diabetic Mother (IDM)Chart · Ch. 17
SGA / IUGRLGA / Macrosomia
DefinitionSGA: weight below the 10th percentile for gestational age (a finding after birth). IUGR (intrauterine growth restriction): poor growth seen on ultrasound before birth.LGA: above the 90th percentile. Macrosomia: 4,000 g or more.
CausePoor placental function: maternal hypertension/preeclampsia, smoking, malnutrition, substance use, multiples, TORCH infections (a group of infections passed to the fetus), chromosomal problemsMaternal diabetes (leading cause), maternal obesity and high weight gain, multiparity, previous big baby, post-term
LookSymmetric (early insult): head, length, and weight all small. Asymmetric / “head-sparing” (late insult): normal head, low weight; large head for body, thin limbs, loose skin, thin umbilical cord (little Wharton’s jelly), often an alert wide-eyed lookBig body with a normal head size (insulin doesn’t cross into the brain); birth injuries: fractured clavicle, brachial plexus injury, cephalohematoma
Main risksHypoglycemia (small glycogen stores), hypothermia (little fat), polycythemia, hypocalcemia, MAS, NECShoulder dystocia, birth trauma, hypoglycemia, polycythemia, jaundice, respiratory distress
Priority careFrequent glucose checks, early feeding, prevent cold stress, daily weights, watch feeding tolerancePrepare for shoulder dystocia, assess for birth injury, monitor blood glucose, early frequent feeds, watch for ruddy color and jaundice
Infant of a diabetic mother (IDM)

During pregnancy, the parent’s high glucose crosses the placenta, so the fetal pancreas makes extra insulin. Insulin is a growth hormone, so the baby grows large and fatty (macrosomia). At birth the glucose supply from the parent stops suddenly, but the baby’s insulin stays high, so blood sugar drops fast. Up to 40% of IDMs become hypoglycemic.

  • Hypoglycemia in the first hours (check glucose per protocol; breastfeed within 1–2 hours)
  • RDS and TTN (transient tachypnea of the newborn): high insulin delays surfactant
  • Polycythemia → hyperbilirubinemia (more RBCs to break down)
  • Hypocalcemia and hypomagnesemia (jitteriness, tetany, seizures look like hypoglycemia)
  • Congenital anomalies 2–4 times more often: heart defects (transposition, VSD), neural tube defects, caudal regression, small left colon
  • Low tone, lethargy, poor feeding; later, higher risk of obesity and diabetes
💡 Exam tip
Both small (SGA) and big (LGA/IDM) babies get hypoglycemia, for opposite reasons: SGA = not enough stored sugar; IDM = too much insulin.
🍬5.8 Neonatal Hypoglycemia, the Glucose Protocol & Glucose Infusion Rate (GIR)Slides 12–13 · Ch. 17 · Blueprint calc

Neonatal hypoglycemia is a blood glucose below 40–45 mg/dL (the exact number depends on age in hours and facility protocol). Glucose is the brain’s fuel, so untreated hypoglycemia can cause seizures and permanent brain injury.

⚠️ At-risk babies (slide 12)
  • Premature and LBW infants: low glycogen stores
  • Infants of diabetic mothers: high insulin
  • SGA, LGA, late preterm, post-term
  • Stressful delivery, cold stress, respiratory distress, sepsis (burn glucose fast)
🔍 Signs (often subtle)
  • Jitteriness, tremors, irritability
  • Lethargy, floppiness, weak or high-pitched cry
  • Poor feeding
  • Exaggerated Moro, cyanosis, temperature instability
  • Severe: apnea, seizures
Nursing interventions (slide 12)
  1. Blood glucose monitoring: check frequently in at-risk babies, especially in the first 24 hours; recheck about 30 minutes after a feed to see if treatment worked
  2. Feeding support: early and frequent feedings (breast or formula); first feed within 1 hour
  3. Buccal glucose gel (40% dextrose rubbed inside the cheek) for persistent low glucose; first-line option in the first 48 hours
  4. IV glucose (D10W, 10% dextrose in water) if the baby can’t keep glucose up orally or is symptomatic
  5. Parent education: feeding patterns and signs of hypoglycemia
Situation (slide 13)Birth to 4 hours4 to 24 hours
RoutineFeed within 1 hour; screen glucose 30 minutes after the first feedFeed every 2–3 hours; screen before each feed
Initial screen lowUnder 25 mg/dL → feed and recheck in 1 hourUnder 35 mg/dL → feed and recheck in 1 hour
Recheck still very lowUnder 25 → IV glucoseUnder 35 → IV glucose
Recheck borderline25–40 → refeed or IV glucose as needed35–45 → refeed or IV glucose as needed
Symptomatic and under 40 mg/dL at any time → IV glucose. Target 45 mg/dL or higher before routine feeds. IV dose: 200 mg/kg (D10W 2 mL/kg) bolus and/or infusion at 5–8 mg/kg/min (80–100 mL/kg/day), aiming for plasma glucose 40–50 mg/dL.
🧮 Calculation: glucose infusion rate (GIR)
The GIR tells you how many milligrams of glucose per kilogram the baby gets each minute.
GIR (mg/kg/min) = (dextrose % × rate in mL/hr) ÷ (6 × weight in kg)
Why 6? D10W has 10 g per 100 mL = 100 mg/mL, so % × 10 = mg/mL; divide by 60 minutes → the constants simplify to 6.
Example 1: 3 kg newborn on D10W at 9 mL/hr → (10 × 9) ÷ (6 × 3) = 90 ÷ 18 = 5 mg/kg/min (within the 5–8 target).
Example 2 (bolus): 3.5 kg baby needs D10W 2 mL/kg → 2 × 3.5 = 7 mL (= 700 mg = 200 mg/kg).
Example 3 (rate from mL/kg/day): 2.4 kg baby ordered 80 mL/kg/day → 80 × 2.4 = 192 mL/day ÷ 24 = 8 mL/hr.
Example 4 (solve for rate): 4 kg IDM, goal GIR 6 on D10W → rate = (6 × 6 × 4) ÷ 10 = 14.4 mL/hr.
⚠️ IV dextrose safety
D10W is the usual peripheral IV concentration in newborns (higher concentrations need a central line). Never stop a dextrose infusion abruptly (rebound hypoglycemia); wean as ordered and keep checking glucose. Hypothermia, respiratory distress, and sepsis all increase glucose use, so fix those too.
💡 Exam tip
Asymptomatic + low glucose → feed first, then recheck. Symptomatic (jittery, lethargic, seizing) or very low → IV dextrose. Memorize the GIR formula for the one calculation question.
💛5.9 Hyperbilirubinemia (Jaundice), Phototherapy & KernicterusSlides 10–11 · Ch. 17 · Chart

Bilirubin is the yellow waste product made when old red blood cells break down. The liver “conjugates” it (changes it into a water-soluble form) so it can leave the body in stool and urine. Hyperbilirubinemia means too much bilirubin in the blood, which shows as jaundice: yellow skin and sclera (whites of the eyes). It becomes visible at about 5 mg/dL and spreads from the head downward as levels rise. 60–70% of term and 80% of preterm babies get some jaundice.

Why newborns are prone to it (Ch. 17)
  • More RBCs for their size, and those RBCs live only 70–90 days (adults: 120)
  • Immature liver: less of the enzyme (glucuronyl transferase) that conjugates bilirubin
  • Few gut bacteria and slow stooling, so bilirubin is reabsorbed from the intestine
Physiologic jaundicePathologic jaundice
OnsetAfter the first 24 hours of lifeWithin the first 24 hours
CoursePeaks day 3 (term), days 5–6 (preterm); resolves by about day 7 without treatmentRises fast (more than 0.2 mg/dL per hour), above the 95th percentile, or lasts beyond 2 weeks; high direct bilirubin
CauseNormal newborn RBC breakdown and immature liverABO incompatibility (parent type O, baby A or B), Rh incompatibility (parent Rh−, baby Rh+), hemolytic disease, G6PD deficiency, bruising/cephalohematoma, infection, polycythemia
MeaningNormal, self-limitingAlways needs evaluation; higher risk of brain damage
🧠 Kernicterus (bilirubin encephalopathy)
Unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin can cross the blood-brain barrier and deposit in brain cells. Early signs: excessive sleepiness, poor feeding, low tone, high-pitched cry. Permanent damage: seizures, cerebral palsy, deafness, intellectual disability, developmental delay. Preventing kernicterus is the whole point of monitoring and treating jaundice.
Nursing interventions (slide 10)
✅ Slide priorities
  • Phototherapy (blue light) as ordered: light changes bilirubin in the skin into a water-soluble form excreted in urine and stool without the liver
  • Frequent feedings: early and frequent breastfeeding (8–12 times/day) so bilirubin leaves through stool
  • Monitor bilirubin levels: TSB (total serum bilirubin) or TcB (transcutaneous, a skin meter)
  • Parent education: how to recognize jaundice; importance of feeding and output (wet and dirty diapers)
💡 Phototherapy care (Ch. 17)
  • Baby in a diaper only; maximum skin exposed
  • Opaque eye shields on (protect the retina); make sure they don’t cover the nose; remove every 4 hours and during feeds to assess and bond
  • Lights 12–16 inches from the baby; change position often
  • Feed every 2–3 hours; monitor I&O and weight (extra water loss through skin)
  • Monitor temperature (risk of overheating)
  • Expected side effects: loose greenish stools, skin rash, dehydration, hyperthermia, lethargy
  • No lotions or oils on the skin (can burn)
  • Bili blanket (fiber-optic): baby can be held and fed; no eye shields needed if used alone
  • Recheck TSB within 24 hours after stopping (rebound)

Other treatments: exchange transfusion (replaces about 85% of the baby’s blood) when phototherapy fails or hemolysis is severe; IVIG (intravenous immune globulin) for isoimmune hemolysis; prevention of Rh disease with RhoGAM (Rh immune globulin) for Rh-negative pregnant people. The direct Coombs test on cord blood shows whether maternal antibodies are coating the baby’s RBCs. A high reticulocyte count (young RBCs) points to hemolysis. Babies discharged before 72 hours need follow-up in 1–2 days.

Breastfeeding-associated jaundice (“not enough milk”)Breast milk jaundice (“something in the milk”)
OnsetEarly: first few daysLate: after the first week; peaks at 2 weeks
CauseIneffective breastfeeding → low intake, dehydration, delayed meconium → bilirubin reabsorbed in the gutBreast milk composition in some people increases bilirubin reabsorption; baby is feeding well
TreatmentBreastfeed 8–12 times/day; no glucose water; supplement with pumped milk or formula only if intake is poor, weight loss is excessive, or the baby is dehydratedContinue breastfeeding in most cases; if very high, briefly pause for formula, then resume. If jaundice lasts beyond 2 weeks, check direct bilirubin to rule out liver problems (cholestasis)
💡 Exam tip
Jaundice in the first 24 hours is always pathologic; report it. The best everyday treatment is feeding more often. During phototherapy: eyes covered, diaper only, turn often, feed often.
🫧5.10 Neonatal Abstinence Syndrome (NAS) & Neonatal Opioid WithdrawalSlides 7–9 · Ch. 17 · Chart

NAS is withdrawal in a newborn whose mother used substances during pregnancy, most often opioids, but also benzodiazepines, alcohol, barbiturates, and others. When the umbilical cord is cut, the baby’s supply suddenly stops. When the cause is opioids, it is also called NOWS (neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome). Drug exposure has to be chronic (not just around delivery) to cause NAS. Symptoms usually start within 24–72 hours but can be delayed up to 2 weeks with methadone, and may last months.

System (slide 7)SignsWhy
CNS (central nervous system)Irritability, tremors, high-pitched cry, hyperreflexia, hypertonia, seizures, poor sleep, frantic fist suckingThe nervous system is over-excited without the drug
GastrointestinalPoor feeding (uncoordinated suck), vomiting, diarrhea, weight loss, excoriated (raw) diaper skinGut becomes hyperactive
Autonomic dysregulationSweating, yawning, nasal stuffiness, sneezing, fever, mottling, tachypneaAutomatic body controls are unstable
Assessment tools (slide 7 and Ch. 17)
  • Finnegan Neonatal Abstinence Scoring tool: points for each symptom, scored every 3–4 hours; high scores guide medication decisions. Criticized as subjective.
  • Eat, Sleep, Console (ESC): a family-centered approach. Can the baby eat 1–1.5 oz or breastfeed well? Sleep 1 hour? Be consoled within 10–20 minutes? If not, the team meets about medication. ESC lowers NICU admissions, medication use, and length of stay.
  • Toxicology: meconium is the best sample (shows use from about 20 weeks); umbilical cord tissue is an alternative; urine shows only recent use. Rule out hypoglycemia and infection, which look similar.
Nursing care (slide 7)
🤱 Nonpharmacologic first
  • Minimize stimulation: quiet, dimly lit room; cluster care
  • Swaddling in flexion, gentle rocking, pacifier
  • Skin-to-skin and rooming-in with parents
  • Small, frequent feedings, upright position, slow-flow nipple, higher-calorie formula (22–24 cal/oz); gavage if suck is ineffective
  • Daily weights; hydration
  • Skin care for diaper area (loose stools)
💊 Medications when needed
  • Morphine: most common first-line
  • Methadone or buprenorphine
  • Phenobarbital or clonidine (add-on)
  • Benzodiazepines for alcohol withdrawal
  • Doses are weaned slowly as scores improve
Effects of specific substances (Ch. 17)
SubstanceEffects on the fetus and newborn
Opioids (heroin, methadone, oxycodone, fentanyl)Withdrawal in 60–90% of exposed babies; growth restriction, lower birth weight and head circumference; symptoms may last up to 6 months
CocaineNarrows placental vessels → placental abruption, preterm labor, growth restriction, stillbirth; newborn irritability, tremors, high-pitched cry, frantic fist sucking; later attention and language problems
AlcoholA teratogen; miscarriage, preterm birth, SGA; fetal alcohol spectrum disorder: small head, short eye openings, thin upper lip, smooth philtrum, learning and attention problems
CannabisLower birth weight; possible effects on attention, reasoning, and school performance; THC stays in breast milk up to 6 weeks
Nicotine / smokingPlacenta previa, abruption, preterm birth, LBW, cleft lip; SIDS risk (no smoking near the baby)
MethamphetamineLimited data; later anxiety, attention and visual-motor problems
SSRIsPossible anxiety, language, or executive-function effects in childhood; linked with PPHN late in pregnancy
🤍 Breastfeeding and substance use (Ch. 17)
Breastfeeding is encouraged for mothers in treatment on methadone or buprenorphine (tiny amounts in milk may ease withdrawal). It is contraindicated with illicit drug use, polydrug use, or HIV (human immunodeficiency virus). Marijuana (THC) stays in milk up to 6 weeks and is discouraged. Some SSRIs are safe while breastfeeding: sertraline (Zoloft) and paroxetine (Paxil) barely transfer to milk, while fluoxetine (Prozac) reaches high levels and is discouraged.
💬 Caring for the family
Give nonjudgmental, honest, supportive care and watch for your own bias. Involve the mother in routine care, start discharge teaching early (calming techniques, feeding, safe sleep, when to get help, maternal depression and relapse resources), and coordinate social work and follow-up. Reporting to child protective services depends on state law.
💡 Exam tip
NAS = high-pitched cry, tremors, poor feeding, sneezing/yawning. Best first interventions: dark quiet room, swaddle, small frequent feeds. Morphine if those aren’t enough.
🫃5.11 Necrotizing Enterocolitis (NEC)Slide 14 · Ch. 17 · Chart

NEC is a severe inflammation of the intestines in which part of the bowel wall is injured by poor blood flow (ischemia) and then dies (necrosis). Dead bowel can perforate (tear), leak bacteria, and cause sepsis and death. It is the most common GI emergency in neonates; over 90% of cases are in preemies, and 90–95% happen after enteral feeding starts. Symptoms usually appear between 3 and 10 days (up to several weeks) of age.

⚠️ Risk factors (slide 14)
  • Prematurity (biggest risk) and SGA
  • Formula feeding (breast milk significantly lowers risk)
  • Prolonged ROM (rupture of membranes) with amnionitis
  • Congenital heart disease
  • Perinatal hypoxia/asphyxia, sepsis, anemia, LBW

Preemies’ guts have weak barriers, slow motility, fewer immune factors, and higher stomach pH.

🔍 Symptoms (slide 14)
  • Abdominal distension: tight, swollen, shiny; visible bowel loops; discoloration
  • Feeding intolerance: vomiting (bilious = green), increased gastric residuals
  • Bloody stools (frank or hidden)
  • Signs of sepsis: lethargy, temperature instability, apnea, bradycardia, hypotension, low urine output
  • Diminished or absent bowel sounds
  • X-ray: gas in the bowel wall (pneumatosis), free air if perforated
Nursing interventions (slide 14 and lecture)
  1. Withhold feedings (NPO) per orders to rest the gut
  2. Gastric decompression: OG tube to low intermittent suction
  3. IV fluids or TPN (total parenteral nutrition)
  4. Medications: antibiotics, analgesics, and medications to support blood pressure as ordered (the slide lists “antihypertensives”)
  5. Monitor: measure abdominal girth every shift (same spot), check residuals before feeds, bowel sounds, stools for blood, vital signs, labs, strict I&O
  6. Prepare for surgery if perforation or necrosis: bowel resection, possibly a temporary ostomy
  7. Parental support: explain NEC, the plan, and the possible need for surgery

Outcomes: many babies recover if caught early, but NEC is fatal in 20–30%. Long-term problems include short bowel syndrome (after much bowel is removed), nutrition problems, poor weight gain, and developmental delay.

💡 Exam tip
Preemie on feeds + distended belly, increased residuals, bloody stool → stop the feeding and notify the provider. Prevention = human milk (EBM or donor milk).
🧠5.12 Intraventricular Hemorrhage (IVH)Slides 15–17 · Ch. 17 · Chart

IVH is bleeding in the brain that starts in the germinal matrix, a highly vascular area next to the lateral ventricles (fluid spaces in the brain) of the developing brain. In preemies these vessels are extremely fragile, and even small swings in blood pressure, blood flow, or oxygen can rupture them. It mainly affects babies under 32 weeks or under 1,500 g (40–60% of very LBW babies). Most happen in the first week (90% within 72 hours). The germinal matrix is mostly gone after 36 weeks, so IVH in term babies is rare.

Grade (slide 15)What it meansOutlook
IBleeding confined to the germinal matrixGrades I–II often resolve with few long-term effects
IIBlood in the ventricle without ventricular dilation
IIIBlood in the ventricle with dilation; clots fill more than 50% of the ventricleGrades III–IV are serious: higher risk of hydrocephalus, cerebral palsy, delays, death
IVBlood extends into brain tissue (parenchyma)

Risk factors: prematurity and LBW, RDS or mechanical ventilation, hypoxia or fluctuating oxygen, rapid volume expansion or hypertension/hypotension, rapid sodium bicarbonate, acidosis, pneumothorax, sepsis, birth trauma. Routine care like suctioning or repositioning can raise intracranial pressure. Antenatal steroids lower the risk.

🔍 Signs (slide 17 and Ch. 17)
  • Can be silent early (mild cases)
  • Apnea, bradycardia, desaturation
  • Lethargy, poor responsiveness, low tone
  • Bulging, tense fontanel (increased ICP, intracranial pressure)
  • Seizures, changes in muscle tone (severe)
  • Sudden drop in hematocrit, pallor, metabolic acidosis, shock
  • Diagnosis: cranial ultrasound in the first week for NICU babies
✅ Nursing interventions (slide 17)
  • Reduce stress: quiet, dark environment; minimal handling
  • Positioning: head midline/neutral, no extreme flexion or extension; HOB (head of bed) flat or slightly raised; keep hips below head during diaper changes
  • Monitor neuro status: vital signs, behavior, LOC (level of consciousness), tone, fontanel, daily head circumference
  • Give IV fluids slowly to avoid blood pressure swings
  • Keep temperature normal; minimize crying
  • Collaborate with neurology/neonatology; support parents
💡 Exam tip
IVH prevention = stable blood pressure and calm baby: midline head, minimal stimulation, slow fluids. A preemie with a sudden bulging fontanel, falling hematocrit, apnea, and bradycardia in week 1 = think IVH.
🦠5.13 Neonatal Infection, Sepsis & Group B Streptococcus (GBS)Chart · Ch. 17 · Slide 20

A newborn’s immature immune system can’t keep an infection in one place, so infections spread through the body quickly (sepsis). Signs are often vague and subtle, so nurses must notice small changes.

⏰ Types of sepsis
  • Early-onset: first 7 days (under 72 hours in babies under 1,500 g); usually passed from the mother (vertical); GBS babies show symptoms by 12–24 hours
  • Late-onset: after 7 days; often hospital-acquired (horizontal); lower death rate
  • Very late-onset: preemies after 3 months with lines and tubes
⚠️ Risk factors
  • Prematurity, LBW
  • Prolonged rupture of membranes (over 18 hours)
  • Maternal fever/chorioamnionitis, maternal UTI (urinary tract infection)
  • Vaginal GBS colonization
  • Invasive procedures, long hospital stay
Body systemSigns of neonatal infection (Ch. 17)
TemperatureTemperature instability: hypothermia (more common in newborns) or fever
RespiratoryApnea, grunting, retractions, tachypnea, cyanosis
CardiovascularBradycardia or tachycardia, hypotension, poor perfusion, pallor, mottling
NeurologicLethargy, irritability, high-pitched cry, low or high tone, seizures, bulging fontanel
GI / skin / metabolicPoor feeding, vomiting, distention; rash, petechiae, jaundice; glucose instability, metabolic acidosis
Workup and treatment
  • Blood culture (the only definitive test), CBC with differential, urine and CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) cultures, serial CRP (C-reactive protein), procalcitonin
  • Obtain cultures first, then start antibiotics immediately: ampicillin + gentamicin (broad coverage)
  • Negative cultures → stop antibiotics at 36–48 hours. Confirmed sepsis → 10–14 days; meningitis → 21 days
  • For an LP (lumbar puncture), hold the baby still in a flexed position
  • Supportive care: respiratory support, glucose and electrolytes, IV fluids, temperature; hand hygiene and standard precautions; teach parents handwashing
Group B Streptococcus (GBS)

GBS is the main cause of newborn sepsis and meningitis in the U.S. About 20–30% of pregnant people carry it in the vagina/rectum without symptoms, and the baby can pick it up during birth. Prevention:

  • Screen all pregnant people at 36 0/7–37 6/7 weeks (vaginal-rectal culture)
  • Positive → IV penicillin in labor (ampicillin is an alternative; cefazolin for low-risk penicillin allergy)
  • Prophylaxis is “adequate” only if given 4 or more hours before birth
  • Unknown status → give antibiotics if preterm labor, ROM 18 hours or longer, or intrapartum fever 38 °C (100.4 °F) or higher
  • Not needed for a planned cesarean before labor with intact membranes
  • Babies of adequately treated mothers don’t need routine antibiotics unless they show signs; healthy term babies can go home after 24 hours if criteria are met
  • Neonatal treatment: penicillin G (or ampicillin)
💡 Exam tip
A newborn with temperature instability, poor feeding, and lethargy = sepsis until proven otherwise. Priority order: cultures → antibiotics (don’t delay antibiotics waiting for results).
❤️‍🩹5.14 Congenital Anomalies: Heart Defects, Structural Defects & Metabolic DisordersChart · Ch. 17 · Slide 20

Birth defects affect 1 in 33 U.S. babies and cause about 20% of infant deaths. Causes include chromosome problems and environmental factors (teratogens such as alcohol, drugs, radiation, maternal diabetes, and TORCH infections).

Generalized heart defects (chart)

Structural heart defects disrupt normal blood flow and oxygenation. Risk factors: genetic and chromosomal abnormalities, maternal infection, diabetes. Signs: cyanosis, murmur, poor feeding (tires and sweats with feeds), tachypnea. Priority interventions: oxygen support, cardiology/surgical consult, monitor perfusion. Every baby gets CCHD (critical congenital heart disease) pulse-oximetry screening before discharge.

DefectWhat it isTreatment
VSD (ventricular septal defect)Hole between the ventricles; the most common heart defectAbout 90% of small ones close alone; digoxin and diuretics for CHF; surgery
ASD (atrial septal defect)Hole between the atriaMay close alone; treat CHF; surgery
Coarctation of the aortaNarrowing of the aortaProstaglandin E1 keeps the ductus open; surgery
Tetralogy of FallotFour defects: VSD, overriding aorta, pulmonary stenosis, right ventricle hypertrophy; cyanoticProstaglandin E1 until surgery; propranolol
Transposition of the great vesselsAorta and pulmonary artery are switched; a medical emergencyTreat acidosis; prostaglandin E1 to keep a PDA open until surgery
🔄 PDA: closing vs. opening the duct
Indomethacin/ibuprofen block prostaglandins to close a PDA in a preemie (5.5). Prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil) keeps the duct open for babies whose survival depends on it (transposition, severe coarctation, tetralogy) until surgery.
Structural and metabolic anomalies (Ch. 17 tables)
AnomalyKey point
Esophageal atresia / TEF (tracheoesophageal fistula)Esophagus doesn’t connect; drooling, choking with feeds; gastric decompression, surgery
Diaphragmatic herniaBelly organs in the chest; severe respiratory distress; stabilize, surgery
Omphalocele vs. gastroschisisOmphalocele: organs out through the umbilicus, covered by a sac. Gastroschisis: organs out through a hole beside (usually right of) the umbilicus, no sac. Both: surgical (sometimes staged) repair
Cleft lip and palateFeeding challenges; surgical repair
Spina bifida (meningocele, myelomeningocele), anencephalyNeural tube defects; surgery (anencephaly is fatal)
DDH (developmental dysplasia of the hip), clubfoot, polydactyly, syndactylyPavlik harness; casting; surgery
PKU (phenylketonuria)Can’t break down phenylalanine; low-phenylalanine diet
GalactosemiaCan’t convert galactose; lactose-free or soy formula
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia, maple syrup urine disease, fatty acid oxidation disordersFound on the newborn genetic/metabolic screen before discharge
💡 Exam tip
Nursing care for any anomaly: depends on type and severity, plus emotional support, support groups, genetic screening before discharge, and follow-up.
🏡5.15 Family-Centered Care, Parent Education & Discharge Planning for High-Risk InfantsSlides 18–19 · Ch. 17 · Blueprint

Neonatal complications affect the whole family, not just the baby (slide 18). Nurses support both, involve parents in care, and help them feel empowered to care for their infant.

👪 Family-centered care (slide 18)
  • Clear, concise explanations of the condition and treatments
  • Signs to watch for after discharge: jaundice, feeding difficulties, breathing problems
  • Support resources: support groups, community resources, follow-up care
  • Encourage bonding: touch, holding, kangaroo care, pumping and bringing breast milk, photos
  • Orient parents to the NICU equipment; praise their involvement
💔 What parents may feel (Ch. 17)
  • Grief for the loss of the “ideal” baby
  • Guilt (mother may think she caused it)
  • Emotional distancing out of fear the baby will die
  • Anger at loss of control; disappointment at leaving without the baby
  • Delayed attachment from separation (raises risk of later neglect)
  • Family disruption: work, siblings, travel
Key takeaways (slide 19)

Early recognition and intervention improve outcomes. Nurses lead assessment, care coordination, and family education. Addressing physical and emotional needs helps recovery and healthy family dynamics. The lecture’s priority list for every complication: monitor vital signs often, keep the baby warm (babies can’t shiver), prevent and watch for infection, keep the baby fed and hydrated, and support the family.

🚑 Transport to a regional NICU (Ch. 17)
Many hospitals can’t care for critically ill newborns, so regional centers exist. The baby is stabilized before transport by a skilled team. During transport: keep the baby warm, support breathing and IV fluids, monitor vital signs, SpO₂, glucose, pain, and response. Developmental care continues: shield eyes from bright light, ear protection in helicopters, gel mattress, nesting with blankets.
🗓️ Preterm clinical pathway (Ch. 17)
Birth to 1 hour: Apgars, dry and warm (hat, plastic wrap, preheated warmer), clear airway, resuscitate as needed, pulse oximetry, temperature every 15–30 minutes. 1–24 hours: gestational age exam, vital signs every 1–2 hours, cardiorespiratory monitor, glucose checks, IV/parenteral nutrition, mother starts pumping, cultures and antibiotics if at risk. 24 hours to discharge: daily weights, kangaroo care, non-nutritive sucking with tube feeds, watch for oral feeding readiness, teach parents feeding, temperature, signs of distress and sepsis, oxygen management, and CPR.
Discharge planning (Ch. 17)
  • Begins at NICU admission; parents involved from day one; interdisciplinary team (physicians, NPs, nurses, social work, OT, case management, lactation, respiratory therapy, nutrition, pharmacy, home health)
  • Baby is stable: steady weight gain, stable temperature in an open crib, tolerating feedings, stable breathing
  • All screens done: eye (ROP), newborn genetic/metabolic screen, CCHD screen, hearing screen
  • Infant car seat challenge for every baby born before 37 weeks: in their own car seat for 90–120 minutes (or the length of the ride, whichever is longer) while maintaining oxygenation, heart rate, and breathing
  • Family readiness: willing and able to give care, financial resources, safe home
Discharge teaching topicIncludes
General careBathing, feeding, diapering, skin care, growth and milestones
SafetyCar seat use, back to sleep, infant CPR (cardiopulmonary resuscitation), babyproofing, shaken baby prevention
EquipmentApnea monitor, oxygen, suctioning (below)
Medications and treatmentsDose, timing, how to give, side effects
Illness signsWhat to report to the provider
Follow-upPediatrician visits, immunizations, specialist and developmental referrals
📟 Home apnea monitor teaching
  • Purpose: alarms for apnea (a pause in breathing of 20 seconds or more) or bradycardia
  • Place leads/belt correctly; check skin under them
  • Keep the monitor on during sleep and whenever unattended; never turn off alarms; keep it plugged in/charged
  • When it alarms: look at the baby first (color, breathing), not the monitor. If not breathing, gently stimulate; if no response, start infant CPR and call 911
  • Know false alarms (loose lead) vs. true alarms; keep a log
  • All caregivers learn infant CPR before discharge
🫧 Home oxygen teaching
  • Use the exact ordered flow rate; don’t increase it on your own (oxygen toxicity: BPD, ROP)
  • Nasal cannula care; check nostrils and cheeks for skin breakdown
  • No smoking or open flames near oxygen; post “oxygen in use” sign; keep 5–10 feet from heat
  • No petroleum-based products near the face (use water-based)
  • Secure tanks upright; know how much is left; have a backup tank and supplier number
  • Signs of respiratory distress to report: grunting, retractions, color change, faster breathing, poor feeding
  • Notify the power company and EMS (emergency medical services) that the home has medical equipment
💡 Exam tip
Apnea monitor alarm → assess the infant first. Home oxygen → no smoking or flames and don’t change the flow rate. Preemie discharge → car seat challenge and infant CPR teaching.
🕊️

Lecture 2: Perinatal Loss and Bereavement Care

Slides 1–14 · Comprehensive nursing strategies for families experiencing loss · Ch. 17 (Loss and Grief)
🤍5.16 Types of Perinatal Loss & the Emotional Impact on FamiliesSlides 2–3

Perinatal loss is the death of a pregnancy or baby around the time of birth, and it also includes losses that families grieve even when no baby has died (like infertility). The lecturer notes the textbook has little on this topic, so the slides and lecture are your main source. Grief is different for every person and family.

Type of loss (slide 2)What it means
Early pregnancy lossMiscarriage (spontaneous loss) and ectopic pregnancy (implants outside the uterus); the lecturer adds molar pregnancy
StillbirthBaby born without a heartbeat at 20 weeks or later
Neonatal deathBaby dies at less than 28 days of life
Medical terminationEnding a pregnancy for medical reasons (fetal or maternal)
Infertility / failed IVFLoss of hoped-for pregnancy, including failed in vitro fertilization
Life-limiting diagnosesConditions diagnosed before or at birth that will shorten the baby’s life, such as trisomy 18 or 13
Emotional impact (slide 3)
👩‍❤️‍👨 Parents
Shock, guilt, depression, PTSD (post-traumatic stress disorder). Loss can also involve adoption or surrogacy situations.
🧒 Siblings
Confusion and behavioral changes, depending on age and development. They need honest, age-appropriate explanations.
👵 Grandparents and extended/chosen family
Helplessness: grieving the baby and watching their own child suffer.
🕯️ Culture and religion
Cultural and religious beliefs influence how grief is expressed, what rituals matter, and decisions about the body.
📖 The lecturer’s example
A 12-year-old sibling, with the parents’ permission, asked to hold their stillborn brother. The nurse sat in quiet presence and silence while the child processed, then answered questions at an age-appropriate level: why the skin color was different, why the skin looked thin, why the head was swollen, and the baby’s sex. Supporting siblings this way is part of the nurse’s role.
💡 Exam tip
Know the cutoffs: stillbirth = 20 weeks or more; neonatal death = under 28 days. Expect grief responses to vary; no single reaction is “normal.”
🌷5.17 Nursing Care During Pregnancy & Perinatal Hospice/Palliative CareSlides 4 & 10 · Lecture
Nursing care during pregnancy (slide 4)
🧭 Anticipatory guidance for high-risk pregnancies
Tell families what to expect so they can prepare emotionally and practically.
📞 Early referral to perinatal hospice
Connect families early with hospice nurses, perinatologists, NICU staff, and support groups.
📝 Birth planning with the family
Plan the birth around comfort, time together, and memory making.
⚖️ Encourage decision-making autonomy
Give facts and information, then allow space for the family to make their own decisions.
Perinatal hospice and palliative care (slide 10 and lecture)

Perinatal hospice is a compassionate model of care for families who choose to continue a pregnancy after a life-limiting fetal diagnosis. It combines palliative care with obstetric and neonatal care and supports the physical, emotional, and spiritual needs of the baby and family. It isn’t widely available, but it can be found.

Slide 10 focusWhat it looks like
Comfort, not cureThe goal is the baby’s comfort and the family’s time together, not aggressive treatment
Support at home or in the hospitalDuring the pregnancy, and even when a family with a stillbirth diagnosis goes home briefly to plan the delivery
Memory-making opportunitiesPhotos, prints, keepsakes, time holding the baby
Symptom management and 24/7 nurse supportComfort measures for the baby; round-the-clock access to a nurse
  • Interdisciplinary team: obstetricians, neonatologists, nurses, chaplains, social workers, palliative care
  • Personalized birth plan focused on comfort for the parent and baby, especially if the baby is expected to live only a short time
  • Addresses grief, guilt, fear, spiritual needs, and counseling; age-appropriate support for siblings and extended family; ongoing bereavement support
  • Common diagnoses: trisomy 13 and 18, certain incompatible congenital heart defects, severe kidney malformations, severe brain malformations
  • Resources mentioned: perinatalhospice.org, Now I Lay Me Down to Sleep (free remembrance photography), bereavement doulas, chaplain services, ACOG perinatal palliative care guidance (ACOG: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists)
🕯️ The heart of perinatal hospice
“Perinatal hospice is about presence, not fixing.” It means walking alongside families and honoring every moment of the baby’s life, no matter how brief.
💡 Exam tip
A family continues a pregnancy after a trisomy 18 diagnosis → the best nursing action is to support their decision and refer early to perinatal hospice/palliative care, not to push termination or false hope.
🕯️5.18 Nursing Care During Labor, Birth & the Postpartum Period: Physical Care & Memory MakingSlides 5–6 · Lecture · Ch. 17
Labor and delivery (slide 5)
📸 Honor birth plans
Naming the baby, photos, who is present, religious rites. Ask; don’t assume.
🤝 Continuity of care
The same nurse when possible, so the family isn’t retelling their story.
⏸️ Minimize interruptions
Cluster care and protect private time.
🧠 Trauma-informed communication
Gentle, clear, unhurried; explain before touching; respect the family’s pace.

As a new nurse you may not know what to say. Being present, therapeutic silence, therapeutic touch, a comforting hug, and allowing families to express grief without judgment are powerful nursing interventions.

Postpartum period (slide 6)
Slide 6Nursing actions
Physical care: bleeding, lactation suppressionThe birthing parent is still a postpartum patient: assess lochia and fundus, vital signs, pain. Milk often still comes in; support lactation suppression (snug supportive bra, cold packs, avoid nipple stimulation/pumping unless donating) or discuss milk donation as an option
Memory making: keepsakes, photosHandprints and footprints, photos (including professional bereavement photography), locks of hair, ID bracelet, crib card, blankets and hats; ask the unit’s bereavement nurse or specialist about available materials
Respect cultural preferencesRituals, washing or dressing the body, who may touch the baby, baptism or other rites, decisions about autopsy and burial
Involve the lactation consultantComfort measures for engorgement, suppression, or donation
After the hospital (lecture)
  • Cuddle Cot: a cooling device that helps preserve the baby’s body so the family can spend more time together
  • Prepare families for autopsy decisions; a medical examiner may be involved if there is any concern for a crime
  • Help with paperwork for funeral services or disposition of the fetus or infant (funeral home, religious organization, cremation); state laws apply
  • Families may go home to a nursery and supplies for a baby who won’t be coming home: anticipate this grief
💡 Exam tip
Postpartum after a stillbirth, don’t forget physical care (fundus, bleeding, breast engorgement). Offer memory making, but let the family choose; keepsakes can be saved for parents who aren’t ready yet.
💬5.19 Infertility, Sick Newborns (Ambiguous Loss) & Communication Best PracticesSlides 7–8 · Lecture
Infertility and sick newborns (slide 7)
🌱 Infertility grief is often unrecognized
It is rarely discussed and can feel taboo. There is no funeral, so others may not see it as a loss.
🏥 NICU stress and ambiguous loss
Ambiguous loss = grieving something that isn’t a death: the loss of the perfect pregnancy, birth, and baby; going home without the infant; a nurse as the main caregiver; needing donor milk instead of breastfeeding.
🩺 Support medical interpretation
NICU technology creates distance. Be the family’s interpreter for diagnoses, equipment, and treatments.
🤱 Encourage bonding and emotional expression
Touch, holding, kangaroo care, participation in care, and permission to feel.
Communication best practices (slide 8)
DoWhy / example
Active listening and reflection“It sounds like you’re feeling…” shows you hear them
Use therapeutic silenceLets the family feel and speak without pressure
Acknowledge the baby by nameHonors the baby as a real person; ask the name if you don’t know it
Avoid clichésNever: “At least you’re young; you can have another baby,” “Everything happens for a reason,” “At least you have other children”
Validate emotions“Anger is a normal part of grief” or “I’m so sorry for the loss of your daughter, Ava”
🚫 Responses to avoid on exams
False reassurance, minimizing (“it was early”), giving advice (“you should try again soon”), changing the subject, and “I know how you feel.”
💡 Exam tip
The best therapeutic response usually names the baby, acknowledges the feeling, and invites the parent to share, such as: “I’m so sorry Liam died. Would you like to tell me about him?”
🌿5.20 Grief Support, Follow-Up, Family Resources & Nursing ResponsibilitiesSlides 9, 11, 12, 14 · Ch. 17
Grief support and follow-up (slide 9)
⏳ Time with the baby
Unrushed time to hold, bathe, dress, and introduce the baby to family (Cuddle Cot helps).
📷 Professional bereavement photos
For example, Now I Lay Me Down to Sleep.
🧑‍⚕️ Counseling referrals
Grief counseling, support groups, mental health care for depression or PTSD.
🏠 Home visits or follow-up calls
Grief doesn’t end at discharge (about 48 hours after birth); some facilities call or visit.
Family resources (slide 11)
  • Share Pregnancy & Infant Loss Support and Resolve (infertility support)
  • Now I Lay Me Down to Sleep (remembrance photography)
  • Grief counseling and support groups
  • Lactation suppression support
  • Local organizations (search resources in your clinical area)
Nursing responsibilities (slide 12)
ResponsibilityMeaning
1. Advocate for respectful policiesTime with the baby, flexible visiting, culturally respectful practices
2. Provide bereavement trainingStaff education on grief care and communication
3. Participate in debriefingsStaff process difficult cases and care for themselves
4. Ensure documentation for continuityDocument the family’s wishes, memory items given, and legal requirements so every caregiver knows the plan
Grief measures from the textbook (Ch. 17)

Signs of grief include sadness, despair, denial, numbness, shock, disbelief, anger, fatigue, and sleep disturbances. Nurses: be present and listen; express empathy and condolences without trite phrases; refer to the baby by name; explain what to expect physically and emotionally; give ample time with the baby before and after death; provide memorabilia; offer the chaplain and explore wishes for baptism or other rites; discuss autopsy, memorial or funeral, and burial or cremation; encourage accepting help; refer to community services and support groups.

💜 Conclusion (slide 14) and the nurse’s own grief
Grief is unique, and nurses are central: promote presence, empathy, and support. The lecturer (an OB nurse for 26 years) says these are often the moments she feels most needed. Students ask whether it’s okay to cry: yes, showing emotion with the family is human, but don’t make it about you. If you can’t cope and the family would need to console you, another nurse should step in.
💡 Exam tip
Expect questions on therapeutic communication, memory making, cultural respect, and referrals. Debriefing is for staff; follow-up calls and counseling are for families.
💊

Blueprint Extra: Medication Safety for Newborns

Blueprint (Pharmacology & Medication Calculations) · ATI example · Ch. 17
💉5.21 Medication Safety for Newborns & Routine Newborn MedicationsBlueprint · ATI · Ch. 17

The blueprint asks you to apply safety measures when giving medications to newborns and women. Newborns are tiny, their livers and kidneys are immature, and a decimal error can be a tenfold overdose, so every dose is checked carefully.

⚠️ Newborn medication safety
  • Weight-based dosing (mg/kg) using the current weight in kilograms; recalculate as weight changes
  • Independent double-check with a second nurse for high-alert drugs (insulin, opioids, IV dextrose, heparin, electrolytes)
  • Watch decimals: no trailing zeros (5 mg, not 5.0 mg) and always a leading zero (0.5 mL, not .5 mL)
  • Use oral syringes for oral meds and small, precise syringes and infusion pumps for IV meds
  • IM injections go in the vastus lateralis (outer thigh), the preferred newborn site
  • Immature kidneys clear drugs slowly: monitor gentamicin levels, urine output, and kidney labs
  • Check IV sites hourly for infiltration (dextrose and calcium damage tissue)
  • Confirm identity with two identifiers (ID band) and check allergies of the birthing parent for drugs given in labor
👩 Safety for women (Module 6 tie-in)
  • Estrogen with a uterus needs a progestin; question estrogen-only orders
  • Screen for estrogen contraindications (clots, unexplained bleeding, breast/uterine cancer, liver disease, untreated hypertension)
  • Check units carefully (mg vs. g for vaginal cream)
  • Bisphosphonates: upright with water; denosumab: dental care
  • Teach clot warning signs and when to call
Routine medications given to every newborn
MedicationWhyHow and when
Vitamin K (phytonadione)Newborns have little vitamin K (sterile gut, low transfer across the placenta), so they can’t make enough clotting factors. Prevents vitamin K deficiency bleedingSingle IM dose in the vastus lateralis, within the first hours of life (ATI: within about 2 hours)
Erythromycin ophthalmic ointmentPrevents ophthalmia neonatorum (eye infection from gonorrhea or chlamydia picked up during birth)Thin ribbon in each lower conjunctival sac from inner to outer corner, within the first hours of life (ATI: within about 2 hours); don’t rinse it out
💡 Exam tip
From your ATI example: vitamin K and eye ointment are important, but warmth (skin-to-skin) comes first. For any newborn dose, the safest answer usually includes weight in kg, a second-nurse check, and the vastus lateralis for IM.

Module 6: Health Promotion & Maintenance: Women’s Health Across the Lifespan & Intimate Partner Violence

This module follows women’s health from puberty to older adulthood: what most often causes death and how to prevent it, how menopause changes the body and how to ease symptoms, which screenings are due at which age, how to protect bones as estrogen falls, and how social factors shape access to care. Lecture 2 covers intimate partner violence: how to recognize it, screen safely, document, report, and connect survivors to help.

🎯

Blueprint focus: perimenopause and menopause symptom management, age- and risk-based screening, barriers like rural access and low health literacy, cardiovascular risk in women, IPV screening in adults and adolescents (including digital abuse), teen dating violence resources, inclusive care for LGBTQ+ and diverse populations, hormone therapy dosage safety, and estrogen indications and effects.

6.1 Health Promotion & Leading Causes of Death6.2 Cardiovascular Disease in Women6.3 Puberty & Adolescent Health6.4 Lifestyle Factors & Obesity6.5 Perimenopause & Menopause6.6 Menopause Symptom Management & HRT6.7 Reproductive & Sexual Health6.8 Preventive Screenings & Immunizations6.9 Osteoporosis6.10 Older Women’s Health & Aging6.11 Nursing Diagnoses & Test Tips6.12 Social Determinants of Health6.13 LGBTQ+ Health & Cultural Humility6.14 IPV: Definition, Scope & Forms6.15 IPV Risk Factors & Red Flags6.16 Cycle of Abuse6.17 Screening, RADAR & Strangulation6.18 Trauma-Informed Care6.19 IPV in Pregnancy & Special Populations6.20 Teen Dating Violence & Alcohol6.21 Documentation, Legal Issues & Resources
🌸

Lecture 1: Women’s Health Promotion Across the Lifespan

Slides 1–16 · Textbook Ch. 18 (Well Women’s Health) · Women’s Preventive Health Chart 2026 · SDOH chart
🌼6.1 Health Promotion & the Top 10 Causes of Death in FemalesSlides 2–3 · Ch. 18

Health promotion is “the process of enabling people to increase control over, and to improve, their health” (WHO, the World Health Organization). In women’s health, it means giving women information and resources to stay well, not just treating illness. The lecturer reminds you that 51% of the population is female, so this applies to every nursing specialty. The nurse’s role is to educate, advocate, and empower at every life stage.

#Cause of death (slide 3)Key point
1Heart disease#1 cause across most age groups. Women often have different symptoms than men (see 6.2)
2CancerEspecially breast and lung; lung cancer is a leading cause of cancer death
3Unintentional injuriesFalls, motor vehicle accidents, poisoning
4Chronic lower respiratory diseaseIncluding COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease)
5StrokeOften from hypertension or emboli; may present differently in women
6Alzheimer’s diseaseIncreases with age; affects more women
7DiabetesComplications include kidney and heart disease
8Kidney diseaseOften related to diabetes and hypertension
9Influenza and pneumoniaGreater risk in older adults
10SuicideRising in younger and middle-aged women

Nursing focus (slide 3): prevention, early detection, education, and lifestyle interventions. The textbook (Table 18-1) shows the top causes shift with age and race: for females 15–24, accidents, suicide, and homicide lead; from about 45 onward, cancer and heart disease dominate; at 85+, heart disease, cancer, and stroke or Alzheimer’s.

Module objectives (slide 2)
  • Use risk factors and preventive screenings to build tailored health plans
  • Apply lifestyle and obesity knowledge to create interventions
  • Explain care strategies for physical and emotional changes in perimenopause and menopause
  • Develop a health promotion plan for older adults based on aging changes
💡 Exam tip
Social media often suggests breast cancer is the top killer of women; it is heart disease. Young women: accidents, suicide, homicide.
❤️6.2 Cardiovascular Disease Risk in Women & Heart Attack/Stroke Warning SignsBlueprint · Ch. 18 · Lecture

The blueprint asks you to educate on cardiovascular disease risk factors specific to women. Heart disease is the #1 killer, yet women’s symptoms are often subtle and different from men’s, so they’re dismissed or delayed. Never write them off.

⚠️ Risk factors to teach
  • Hypertension and high cholesterol
  • Diabetes (raises heart risk more in women than men)
  • Obesity and physical inactivity
  • Smoking and secondhand smoke
  • Menopause: falling estrogen removes some heart protection
  • Pregnancy complications such as preeclampsia and gestational diabetes
  • Excess alcohol, stress, depression, family history, older age
✅ Risk reduction (Ch. 18)
  • Heart-healthy diet: vegetables, fruits, whole grains, fiber, low-fat dairy, fish; low saturated fat and sodium
  • 150 minutes/week of moderate activity (brisk walking, swimming, biking, dancing)
  • Healthy weight; no smoking or vaping
  • Limit alcohol to 1 drink/day
  • Blood pressure checks and cholesterol/diabetes screening (6.8)
  • Treat diabetes, hypertension, and high lipids
🫀 Heart attack warning signs in women (Ch. 18)
  • Unusually heavy pressure on the chest
  • Sharp upper body pain in the neck, back, and jaw
  • Severe shortness of breath
  • Cold sweats (not menopausal hot flashes)
  • Unusual or unexplained fatigue
  • Unfamiliar dizziness or lightheadedness
  • Unexplained nausea or vomiting
🧠 Stroke warning signs
  • Sudden numbness or weakness of the face, arm, or leg, especially one side
  • Sudden trouble seeing in one or both eyes
  • Sudden trouble walking, dizziness, loss of balance or coordination
  • Sudden severe headache with no known cause
Call 911 right away; time matters.
💡 Exam tip
A 58-year-old woman with unexplained fatigue, nausea, and jaw or back pain may be having a heart attack even without crushing chest pain. Treat it as cardiac until proven otherwise.
🌱6.3 Puberty & Adolescent HealthSlide 4 · Ch. 18 · Lecture

Puberty is when a person becomes sexually mature and able to reproduce. In girls it usually starts between ages 8 and 13, with a growth spurt that starts at the feet and ends with the face. It’s triggered by a hormone chain: the hypothalamus releases GnRH (gonadotropin-releasing hormone) → the anterior pituitary releases gonadotropins → the ovaries make estrogen → secondary sex characteristics develop.

Milestone (slide 4)TermNotes
Breast developmentThelarcheUsually the first visible sign of puberty
Pubic and axillary hair growthAdrenarcheFollows breast development
First menstruationMenarcheAbout 2–2.5 years after puberty begins; puberty is complete when periods are regular
Emotional and social growth—Hormone shifts trigger emotional changes; identity, self-esteem, and peer relationships develop
🩺 Nursing role (slide 4)
Normalize changes, teach hygiene, give emotional support. Provide truthful, scientific explanations and anticipatory guidance about what’s coming (periods, hygiene, body changes) so adolescents aren’t afraid, and foster a healthy body image. Many teens don’t get this information at home, so the nurse may be a safe, trusted adult, especially the school nurse.
