Adolescent health risks (Ch. 18)

Adolescence (ages 12–19) brings physical, cognitive (concrete to abstract thinking), and psychosocial (identity) development. Health issues include menstrual disorders, acne, eating disorders (obesity, anorexia, bulimia), STIs (sexually transmitted infections; chlamydia and gonorrhea are common), teen pregnancy, bullying (20% electronically bullied), and mental health problems. The leading causes of death for females 15–19 are unintentional injuries, suicide, and homicide.

2019 Youth Risk Behavior Survey, high school females (Ch. 18)%
Persistent feelings of sadness or hopelessness46.6%
Seriously considered attempting suicide24.1%
Attempted suicide11.0%
Experienced sexual dating violence / physical dating violence12.6% / 9.3%
Ever physically forced to have sex11.4%
Used a condom the last time they had sex49.6%
💡 Exam tip
Order of puberty: thelarche → adrenarche → menarche (“breasts, hair, period”). Nursing = normalize, educate, support.
🥗6.4 Lifestyle Factors & Obesity RisksSlide 5 · Ch. 18
Lifestyle factor (slide 5)Recommendation (slide + Ch. 18)
NutritionWhole foods, lean protein, limit sugars; vegetables, fruits, whole grains, fiber, low-fat dairy, fish; low saturated fat and sodium (use MyPlate). 3 servings/day of calcium-rich foods (yogurt, milk, cheese, broccoli, kale) to protect bone
Exercise150 minutes/week of moderate activity, including weight-bearing exercise (slows bone loss, builds strength and balance). Lowers risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, colon and breast cancer, falls, and depression. Check with the provider before starting a new program
Smoking cessationTobacco is a leading cause of heart disease and cancer. In pregnancy it raises risk of preterm birth, low birth weight, miscarriage, and fetal lung/brain damage. Avoid secondhand smoke and e-cigarettes (nicotine; THC vapes linked to lung injury)
Alcohol (Ch. 18)No more than 1 drink/day for women; none in pregnancy (FASD, fetal alcohol spectrum disorder, and more). Binge drinking (5 drinks) increases risk of sexual assault
Sun/UV protection (Ch. 18)Protective clothing, hat, sunglasses, SPF 15 or higher, avoid sun 10 a.m.–2 p.m.
Injury prevention (Ch. 18)Seat belts, speed limits, no drinking and driving (MVAs, motor vehicle accidents, kill younger women); fall prevention for 65+ (falls are the leading cause of injury death in older women)
Obesity

About 40–46% of U.S. women are obese. Classes: class 1 BMI 30–35, class 2 BMI 35–40, class 3 BMI over 40 (BMI = body mass index). The slide stresses that obesity increases the risk of heart disease, diabetes, breast and endometrial cancer, and infertility. The textbook adds hypertension, stroke, gallbladder disease, sleep apnea, osteoarthritis of the knee, hip, and back, abnormal periods, high-risk pregnancies, miscarriage, and macrosomic babies.

🎗️ HPV and the HPV vaccine (Ch. 18)
HPV (human papillomavirus) is the most common sexually transmitted virus and the main cause of cervical cancer and genital warts (also vulvar, vaginal, penile, anal, and throat cancers). The Gardasil 9 vaccine is given IM: 2 doses if started before age 15 (second dose 6–12 months later); 3 doses if started at 15 or older (at 0, 1–2, and 6 months). Teach: finish the series, it does not prevent other STIs, and cervical screening is still needed.
💡 Exam tip
Know the numbers: 150 minutes/week, 1 drink/day, SPF 15+, BMI 30 = obesity. Obesity is specifically tied to endometrial and breast cancer and infertility.
🔥6.5 Perimenopause & Menopause: The Hormonal Shift and Its SymptomsSlides 6–7 · Ch. 18 · Lecture

Starting in a woman’s late 30s, the quality and number of eggs decline, so the ovaries make less estrogen and progesterone. The symptoms that follow are “menopause symptoms.” They range from none to severe. The lecturer notes most OB-GYNs get little training in menopause, so nurses can play a huge role in education and support; every woman will go through it.

StageWhat happens
PerimenopauseThe transition, usually in the 40s, lasting 4–8 years: irregular cycles, mood swings, vasomotor symptoms, sleep problems. Pregnancy is still possible, so contraception is still needed
Menopause12 months without a menstrual period; average age 51 (range 45–55)
PostmenopauseThe time after menopause; no longer fertile
🔥 Physical symptoms
  • Hot flashes (the key, most common symptom): blood vessels near the skin dilate in response to hormone changes, causing sudden warmth in the upper body and face, redness, sweating. Triggers: warm rooms, alcohol, hot or spicy foods, caffeine, stress
  • Night sweats: hot flashes during sleep that soak bedding
  • Sleep disturbance
  • Vaginal dryness and atrophy (thin, dry tissue; patients describe “sandpaper”) → dyspareunia (painful intercourse)
  • Irregular periods, heavier or lighter flow
  • Thinning hair, dry skin, weight gain at the waist and hips, palpitations
  • Lecture: joint pain and frozen shoulder
💭 Emotional symptoms
  • Mood swings, irritability
  • Brain fog, forgetfulness
  • Anxiety, panic attacks
  • Depression, lack of energy, trouble coping
  • Decreased libido and sexual well-being
🚨 Red flag
Any vaginal bleeding after menopause is a concern for reproductive (endometrial) cancer and must be reported and evaluated (lecture).
💡 Exam tip
Menopause = 12 months with no period. Perimenopause = irregular cycles, can still get pregnant. Hormone change = ↓ estrogen. Key symptom = hot flashes.
🌡️6.6 Menopause Symptom Management & Menopausal Hormone Therapy (HRT/MHT)Slides 7 & 14 · Ch. 18 · Blueprint calc

Treatment has three approaches: lifestyle changes (always first-line), alternative medicine, and menopausal hormone therapy (MHT, often called HRT, hormone replacement therapy). The slide summary: lifestyle changes, water-based lubricants, and HRT (estrogen + progesterone if a uterus is present).

SymptomNursing teaching (Ch. 18)
Hot flashesAvoid alcohol, hot drinks, spicy foods, warm rooms, smoking; dress in layers; avoid wool/synthetics; use fans. Nonhormonal meds: low-dose SSRIs such as fluoxetine, gabapentin, clonidine
Night sweatsCotton nightwear and sheets, cool room, fan over the body, cool shower before bed
Sleep disturbanceRegular bedtime; no TV/computer in bed; phone in another room; dark, quiet, cool bedroom; loose breathable clothes; eat dinner early; avoid alcohol and caffeine near bedtime (wine before bed makes sleep worse)
Vaginal drynessWater-based lubricants, vaginal moisturizers, estrogen vaginal cream; soy flour and flaxseed may help
MoodDaily exercise, limit alcohol, natural light or light box; psychotherapy and antidepressants if needed
Alternative medicineHerbal supplements, acupuncture, biofeedback, and hypnosis (Ch. 18). Teach women to tell their provider about any herbal products, since supplements can interact with medicines
General lifestyle8 hours of sleep, balanced diet, weight loss if overweight, exercise, no caffeine/alcohol/smoking
Menopausal hormone therapy
💊 Which regimen?
  • No uterus (hysterectomy) → estrogen alone (oral, transdermal, vaginal)
  • Has a uterus → estrogen + progesterone (progestin). Estrogen alone makes the endometrium (uterine lining) grow and raises endometrial cancer risk; progesterone protects it
  • Start at the lowest effective dose; transdermal is preferred; reevaluate every year
  • Lecture: HRT may include testosterone; newer evidence suggests benefits for heart, bone, and possibly Alzheimer’s risk, unlike older fears
🚫 Estrogen contraindications
  • Unexplained vaginal bleeding
  • Liver disease, gallbladder disease
  • Blood-clotting disorders, pulmonary embolism
  • Untreated hypertension
  • Uterine or breast cancer (estrogen-dependent cancers)
Teach signs of clots to report: one-sided calf pain/swelling, chest pain, shortness of breath.
🧪 Slide 14 NCSBN-style examples
1. A 52-year-old reports sleep disturbances and hot flashes. Priority? Cool room (not wine before bed, a psychiatry referral, or night exercise). Nonpharmacologic sleep hygiene comes first.
2. A postmenopausal woman with a uterus is prescribed estrogen-only therapy. Action? Notify the provider/question the order, because unopposed estrogen raises endometrial cancer risk.
🧮 Calculation practice: hormone therapy dosages
Dose ordered ÷ dose on hand × quantity = amount to give
Example 1: Conjugated estrogen (Premarin) 1.25 mg PO daily is ordered; tablets are 0.625 mg → 1.25 ÷ 0.625 = 2 tablets.
Example 2: Medroxyprogesterone acetate 5 mg PO on days 15–28; tablets are 2.5 mg → 5 ÷ 2.5 = 2 tablets daily on those days.
Example 3: Estradiol vaginal cream 0.5 g daily for 2 weeks, then twice weekly → total for the first 2 weeks = 0.5 × 14 = 7 g.
Example 4 (Premphase cycle): estrogen 0.625 mg on days 1–14, then estrogen 0.625 mg + medroxyprogesterone 5 mg on days 15–28 → the client takes medroxyprogesterone on 14 days of each 28-day cycle.
Safety: check that a client with a uterus also has a progestin ordered; use the lowest effective dose; recheck units (mg vs. g).
💡 Exam tip
Lifestyle first (cool room, layers, avoid triggers), then meds. Uterus present = estrogen + progesterone. Postmenopausal bleeding = report.
💞6.7 Reproductive & Sexual Health Across the LifespanSlide 8 · Ch. 18 · Lecture
💊 Contraceptive options across the lifespan
Women need guidance from first sexual activity through perimenopause (pregnancy is possible until menopause is confirmed). Covered in depth in the next module.
💉 HPV vaccination (ages 11–26/45)
Routine at 11–12; catch-up through 26; shared decision-making for 27–45 (2026 chart). Ch. 18 lists women 19–26.
🛡️ STI prevention and screening
Barrier methods (condoms), screening based on risk (see 6.8); the higher the risk behavior, the more often you screen.
🏳️‍🌈 LGBTQ+ inclusive care
Affirm gender identity and create safe environments; these patients often face bias (see 6.13).

Sexual health (WHO) is physical, emotional, mental, and social well-being related to sexuality, not just the absence of disease, including the possibility of pleasurable and safe experiences free of coercion, discrimination, and violence. Women should feel free to discuss low sexual desire, IPV, and dyspareunia with providers, use methods to prevent STIs and unintended pregnancy, and talk with partners about their needs.

🗣️ The lecturer’s key message: start the conversation
Talking about sex makes many nurses uncomfortable, but every patient, in every setting, has questions about sexual health; most won’t ask. Examine your own discomfort and bias and open the conversation yourself: a young person starting to be sexually active, every postpartum patient (STIs, contraception, what sex may feel like after birth), and patients recovering from surgery or a cardiac event (when they can resume sexual activity). Include it in every discharge teaching.
Sexual health in older women (Ch. 18)

Older women stay sexually active. Age doesn’t affect the capacity for orgasm, though intensity and frequency may decrease. Falling estrogen causes vaginal dryness, burning, itching, and pain with penetration; women in their 60s have about half the testosterone of women in their 20s, which can lower libido. Promote fitness, local vaginal estrogen, and open discussion with partners.

💡 Exam tip
The nurse should initiate sexual health discussions nonjudgmentally. HPV vaccine teaching: complete the series; still get Pap/HPV screening; it doesn’t prevent other STIs.
🩺6.8 Preventive Screenings & Immunizations Across the LifespanSlide 10 · Ch. 18 · 2026 chart

Screenings find problems early, before symptoms, when treatment works best. They are based on age and risk factors. The lecturer doesn’t expect you to memorize every cell, but you should know the general schedule well enough to teach patients.

📝 Note: the slide’s DXA row
On slide 10 the DXA row is shifted: it shows “frequency based on history” under ages 19–39 and 40–49 and leaves 50–64 and 65+ blank. The textbook (Table 18-2) shows the reverse, which is correct: DXA is based on history and osteoporosis risk from age 50 on, and the 2026 chart recommends it for all women 65+. This sheet uses the textbook version.
📝 Note: slide vs. the 2026 guideline chart
For the exam, use the slide/textbook schedule and the lecturer’s comments. Your supplemental 2026 chart (USPSTF, U.S. Preventive Services Task Force; CDC/ACIP, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention / Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices; ACS, American Cancer Society; ACOG; ADA, American Diabetes Association) shows current updates: cervical screening begins at 21 (Pap every 3 years 21–29; HPV testing every 5 years preferred 30–65; stop at 65 with adequate prior screening); mammogram every 2 years from 40 through 74; colorectal screening begins at 45; DXA for all women 65+ (earlier if postmenopausal with risk factors); diabetes screening from 35 if overweight; HIV at least once 15–65; hepatitis C once 18–79; annual low-dose CT for lung cancer if eligible; BP every 3–5 years if low risk under 40, yearly after.
🎀 Breast cancer screening (Ch. 18)
  • Average risk → mammogram. High risk (BRCA1/BRCA2 gene mutation or lifetime risk 20% or more) → MRI + mammogram
  • Monthly self-breast exams are no longer recommended, but women should know their breasts and report changes: lump, dimpling, skin color/texture change, nipple pulling in, clear or bloody nipple discharge
  • Mammogram day: no deodorant, perfume, lotion, or powder on breasts or underarms (causes shadows); tell staff about implants; expect brief squeezing
🔬 Cervical screening rules (Ch. 18)
  • Women over 65 can stop if no precancerous cells in the past 10 years
  • Total hysterectomy → stop, unless done for cervical cancer or precancer
  • HPV-vaccinated women still follow routine screening
Adult immunizations (Ch. 18 and 2026 chart)
VaccineRecommendation
InfluenzaEvery year
COVID-19Per current CDC recommendations
Tdap/Td (tetanus, diphtheria, pertussis)One adult Tdap, then Td or Tdap every 10 years; Tdap in each pregnancy
HPVCh. 18: 19–26; 2026 chart: catch-up through 26, shared decision 27–45
MMR (measles, mumps, rubella)1 dose if not immune (ages 19–59 per Ch. 18)
Varicella (chickenpox)2 doses 4–8 weeks apart if not immune
Shingles (Shingrix, herpes zoster)Age 50+
PneumococcalAge 65+ or earlier with risk conditions
Hepatitis B; RSVHep B universal 19–59; RSV at 75+ or by risk (2026 chart)
🧭 Behavioral screening (2026 chart)
Screen all adults for depression (including pregnancy and postpartum), alcohol use, tobacco use, and obesity; anxiety for ages 19–64; and IPV for women of reproductive age.
💡 Exam tip
Quick pearls: 21 cervical screening · 35 diabetes screen if overweight · 40 mammogram + baseline eye exam · 45 colorectal · 50 Shingrix · 65 DXA for all + pneumococcal.
🦴6.9 Osteoporosis: Risk, Diagnosis, Prevention & MedicationsSlide 9 · Ch. 18

Osteoporosis is loss of bone mass when the body breaks down more bone than it builds. Bone mass starts falling after about 35 and drops fastest in the first 2–3 years after menopause (estrogen protects bone). 80% of Americans with osteoporosis are women. It raises the risk of vertebral and hip fractures.

📊 Diagnosis: DXA scan T-score
A DXA (dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry) scan measures bone density in the hip, spine, and forearm and compares it with a young healthy adult:
  • −1 or higher: normal
  • −1 to −2.5: osteopenia (low bone density, at risk)
  • −2.5 or lower: osteoporosis
🔍 Signs
  • Back pain from a fractured or collapsed vertebra
  • Loss of height
  • Stooped posture (kyphosis)
  • Fractures from minor falls (fragility fractures)

Risk factors: white race; thin, small-boned build (BMI 20 or less, under 127 lb); family history of hip fracture; smoking; inactivity; low calcium and vitamin D (vitamin D helps absorb calcium); 3 or more drinks/day; long-term corticosteroids (over 3 months), aromatase inhibitors, PPIs (proton pump inhibitors); eating disorders; weight-loss surgery.

Daily calcium (Ch. 18)Amount
Girls 9–181,300 mg
Women 19–501,000 mg
Women 51+1,200 mg
Vitamin D, women 50+600–1,000 IU (Table 18-4: 600–800 units)

Calcium-rich foods: canned sardines (3 oz) 325 mg, plain low-fat yogurt (4 oz) 310 mg, cheddar (1.5 oz) 307 mg, calcium-fortified OJ, 2% milk, or almond/soy/rice milk (8 oz) 300 mg, salmon 181 mg, frozen kale 180 mg. Prevention: start calcium-rich eating by age 9, weight-bearing exercise (walking, jogging, dancing, weights) 3–4 times/week, no smoking, limit alcohol.

Pharmacotherapy (Ch. 18)

ACOG recommends medication for women with a fragility (low-impact) fracture, a T-score of −2.5 or lower, or risk factors with a T-score below −1.5.

DrugKey facts
Bisphosphonates: alendronate (Fosamax), ibandronate (Boniva), risedronate (Actonel), zoledronate (Reclast)Stop bone breakdown (resorption). Side effects: muscle aches, GI irritation, esophageal ulcers. Alendronate: prevention 5 mg/day or 35 mg/week; treatment 10 mg/day or 70 mg/week. Ibandronate 150 mg monthly. Zoledronate IV yearly (treatment)
Raloxifene (Evista) (estrogen-receptor modulator)Estrogen-like effect on bone. Risk: blood clots (VTE), leg cramps, stroke
Hormone therapy: Premarin (no uterus), Premphase (uterus)Contraindicated with estrogen-dependent cancer
Denosumab (Prolia)60 mg subcut every 6 months; for those who can’t take bisphosphonates (kidney problems). Risk: osteonecrosis of the jaw (routine dental care), low calcium
Teriparatide (Forteo)20 mcg subcut daily for high fracture risk or steroid-related osteoporosis
💊 Alendronate (Fosamax) teaching
Take in the morning on an empty stomach, at least 30 minutes before breakfast, with a full 8 oz glass of plain water (not juice, coffee, or tea); take it sitting or standing and stay upright for at least 30 minutes to prevent the pill from sticking in or refluxing into the esophagus and causing ulcers.
🏠 Nursing teaching plan (Ch. 18)
Risk factors; fall prevention (remove throw rugs, clear floors, light stairways, grab bars by the tub and toilet, yearly eye exams, limit alcohol, wear shoes inside and out); what to expect with a DXA scan; calcium and vitamin D foods; weight-bearing activity; medications; smoking and alcohol.
💡 Exam tip
T-score −2.5 = osteoporosis. Alendronate = water, empty stomach, upright 30 minutes. Loss of height in an older woman = think vertebral compression fracture.
👵6.10 Health Promotion for Older Women: Aging Changes, Falls, Medications & DrivingSlide 9 · Ch. 18 Table 18-4

Health promotion for older adults aims to minimize the effects of normal aging and maximize quality of life. Slide 9: common changes are ↓ bone mass, vision, muscle strength, and libido; nursing focus is fall prevention (home safety, balance exercises), osteoporosis (calcium/vitamin D, walking, DXA scan), and sleep and sexual health (cool room, lubricants). The lecture adds sleep and cognitive shifts and chronic illness risk.

Aging changeEffectHealth promotion
↓ Muscle mass↓ StrengthStrength training, healthy diet
↓ Total body water, ↓ kidney function↑ Dehydration riskAt least 8 glasses of fluid spread through the day
↓ Smell and taste↓ AppetiteHealthy teeth/gums; colorful food presentation
↓ Metabolism↑ Body fat, ↓ muscleFewer calories, more activity, strength training
↓ T-cells, ↓ lung elasticity↑ Infections, pneumonia, cancerHand hygiene, yearly flu vaccine, pneumococcal vaccine, cancer screening
High-frequency hearing loss; ↓ peripheral vision, depth perception, cataracts↓ Speech recognition, ↓ eyesightHearing and eye evaluations; sunglasses when driving
↓ Intestinal motility↑ ConstipationDaily exercise, fluids, fruit/vegetables/whole grains/probiotics
Weak bladder wall, prolapse, cystoceleFrequency, incontinence, cystitisKegel exercises, ideal weight, bladder training, double and timed voiding
Leg weakness, vertigo, vision changes, hypotension, confusion, foot problems↑ Fall riskFall risk evaluation, home safety (lighting, no loose rugs, grab bars), adjust medications, flat nonskid shoes, yearly vision exams
↓ Baroreceptor sensitivityOrthostatic hypotensionRise slowly from sitting or lying
↓ Liver mass and blood flow, ↓ GFR↑ Adverse drug reactionsTell providers about all prescription, OTC (over-the-counter), and herbal products; follow directions
↓ Prefrontal cortex and hippocampusChanges in learning and memoryControl BP and diabetes, vitamin B12 2.4 mcg, exercise, mental stimulation, social connection
💊 Medication safety
Older adults are more sensitive to drugs (slower metabolism and kidney/liver function) and take more medicines (more interactions). Keep a list of all meds (name, dose, reason) and bring it to every visit; report side effects; dispose of expired meds at the pharmacy.
🦷 Skin, nutrition, mouth
Dry skin: fluids, daily lotion, humidifier, mild soap, warm (not hot) water, sun protection. Nutrition barriers: living alone, depression, mouth pain, limited income, altered taste. Mouth: brush twice, floss daily, dentist every 6 months.
🚗 Signs driving is no longer safe (Ch. 18)
Trouble seeing or following signals and signs; stopping at green lights; confusion at signals; running stop signs or red lights; getting lost in familiar places; new dents and scrapes on the car or garage; slower responses; trouble moving the foot from gas to brake. Health promotion: yearly eye exams, no drinking and driving, avoid night or bad-weather driving, limit distractions, avoid driving on drowsy medications.
💡 Exam tip
Fall prevention is the top older-adult safety priority: remove rugs, add grab bars and lighting, wear nonskid shoes, rise slowly, review medications.
📋6.11 Nursing Diagnoses, Outcomes, NCLEX Test Tips & Discussion QuestionsSlides 11, 13–16 · Ch. 18

The lecturer asks you to focus on nursing concerns (what the nurse can treat and teach), not medical diagnoses.

Nursing diagnosis (slide 11)Matching outcome (Ch. 18)
Knowledge deficit related to menopausal changesWoman verbalizes menopausal changes and ways to decrease symptoms
Risk for disturbed sleep pattern related to night sweatsWoman verbalizes three strategies to improve sleep
Risk for falls related to impaired balanceWoman develops a health promotion plan based on aging changes
Readiness for enhanced self-care—
At risk for adverse health conditions related to lack of knowledge of health promotionSlide outcome: woman verbalizes at least 2 lifestyle changes to reduce risk
🎯 NCLEX/NCSBN test plan tips (slide 13)
  1. Use the nursing process (ADPIE): assessment, diagnosis, planning, implementation, evaluation
  2. Prioritize safety and ABCs (airway, breathing, circulation)
  3. Know normal vs. abnormal (for example, when osteoporosis risk becomes a concern)
  4. Educate and empower
  5. Look for clue words (“first,” “priority,” “most important”)
💬 Discussion questions (slide 15)
  1. Barriers in rural/low-income settings?
  2. Education differences by socioeconomic status?
  3. Culturally sensitive contraception teaching?
  4. Supporting LGBTQ+ women?
  5. Fall prevention priorities in older adults?
Answers are woven through 6.10, 6.12, and 6.13.
🌟 Final takeaways (slide 16)
You aren’t just teaching symptoms; you’re empowering women to live healthier, more autonomous lives. Study smart, think holistically, advocate fiercely. Nursing is rooted in integrity and character: you are caring for someone’s mother, sister, daughter, or partner.
🤔 Textbook case study (adapted): Kathy, 65, retired teacher

BP 124/96, BMI about 27, family history of type 2 diabetes, stroke, and colon cancer; DXA shows osteopenia; sedentary (TV, sewing, reading); diet high in fat and carbs, low in fruits and vegetables.

  • Priority learning needs: weight-bearing exercise (osteopenia, weight, heart), heart-healthy and calcium/vitamin D–rich diet, blood pressure follow-up, diabetes and colorectal screening, fall prevention.
  • Teaching plan: quiet, well-lit space; assess what she already knows and her preferences; start with one or two goals; use teach-back to evaluate.
💡 Exam tip
When several answers are “right,” choose the safety/ABC answer, then the nonpharmacologic answer, then teaching.
🌍6.12 Social Determinants of Health (SDOH) & Barriers to CareSlide 12 · SDOH chart · Blueprint

Social determinants of health (SDOH) are the conditions where people live, learn, work, and age (income, education, housing, transportation, racism, and access to care) that shape health more than biology alone. Nurses see the whole person in their whole environment and connect them with services: interpreters, community resources, telehealth.

SDOH categoryConsiderations in women’s healthNursing implications
RaceDisparities in maternal morbidity, hypertension, cancer screening; Black women have higher maternal mortalityCulturally competent care, screen for disparities, advocate for equitable access
EthnicityHispanic and Indigenous populations may face language barriers and less preventive careUse interpreters, assess health beliefs, address health literacy, culturally appropriate education
AgeAdolescents need sexual health education; older adults need osteoporosis and chronic disease screeningTailor care to developmental stage; age-specific screenings
ReligionBeliefs influence contraception, abortion, and end-of-life decisionsRespect beliefs, spiritual assessment, chaplain services
SexualityLGBTQ+ people may delay care due to discrimination or lack of provider understandingInclusive environments, affirming language, know unique risks (STIs, mental health)
GenderTransgender women may struggle to access gender-affirming and reproductive careUnderstand gender identity, avoid assumptions, respectful care
Socioeconomic statusLow income → trouble with transportation, insurance, medications, healthy foodCommunity resources, social needs assessment, sliding-scale options, referrals
Geographic locationRural women have limited access to specialists and reproductive servicesTelehealth, advocate for mobile clinics and outreach
EducationLimited education → lower health literacy, less preventive careTeach-back method, assess literacy, clear simple materials
Disability statusPhysical and systemic barriers to routine carePhysical accessibility, respectful communication, interdisciplinary coordination
📚 Low health literacy: what works
Teach-back (“Tell me in your own words how you’ll take this”), plain language without jargon, short chunks, pictures, demonstrations, and checking understanding rather than asking “Do you understand?”
💡 Exam tip
Rural barrier → telehealth/mobile clinic. Language barrier → professional interpreter (not family). Low literacy → teach-back.
🏳️‍🌈6.13 LGBTQ+ Women’s Health & Cultural HumilitySlide 8 · Ch. 18 · Blueprint

LGBTQ+ (lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, and others) individuals experience health disparities from societal stigma, discrimination, and denial of civil rights. Being LGBTQ+ is not unhealthy; social factors block easy access to care. Lesbian women face barriers such as lack of insurance, fear of negative reactions from providers, and providers who don’t understand their health needs, so they see providers less often and seek care later.

Health issue (Ch. 18)Why
Cancer (breast, cervical, endometrial, ovarian)Higher rates of smoking, alcohol use, and obesity; less screening
Obesity and heart diseaseHigher BMI and smoking rates
PCOS (polycystic ovary syndrome)Appears more often; raises risk of menstrual problems, infertility, insulin problems, heart disease
OsteoporosisSmoking, alcohol, antidepressant use
Tobacco, alcohol, substance useHigher than in heterosexual women
Domestic violenceOccurs in lesbian relationships too; all women need screening; few agencies focus on same-sex IPV
✅ Nursing actions
  • Be a nonjudgmental, safe place to ask questions
  • Affirm gender identity; use the patient’s name and pronouns; inclusive forms and language (“partner”)
  • Create a welcoming, safe environment
  • Address psychosocial determinants of health
  • Teach: routine screening and immunizations, exercise, healthy diet, smoking cessation, limiting alcohol, safety planning for IPV, osteoporosis risk reduction
🪞 Cultural humility
Ongoing self-reflection and education to recognize your own assumptions and biases. Cultural competence implies “I am the expert”; cultural humility implies “You are the expert” on your own life and culture (Rudd, 2018).
💡 Exam tip
The best response to an LGBTQ+ patient is open, affirming, and nonassumptive: ask about partners with gender-neutral language and screen everyone for IPV.
🛡️

Lecture 2: Intimate Partner Violence (IPV): Nursing Roles in Identification, Care, and Prevention

Slides 1–19 · Ch. 18 (IPV Screening; Caring for Patients Who Have Experienced Trauma) · CDC (2024)
📢6.14 IPV: Definition, Scope of the Problem & Forms of AbuseSlides 2–4 · Ch. 18

Intimate partner violence (IPV) is physical, sexual, or psychological abuse or stalking by a current or former partner (CDC, 2024). It happens in heterosexual and same-sex couples of every race, age, income, and religion. The lecturer notes the textbook has limited information, so the slides, lecture, and course resources are key.

📊 Scope (slide 3)
  • 1 in 4 women and 1 in 10 men experience IPV in their lifetime
  • IPV can escalate during pregnancy
  • Leads to chronic illness, mental health issues, and adverse fetal outcomes (stress in pregnancy affects the baby and child)
🗂️ Forms of IPV (slide 4)
  • Physical: hitting, choking
  • Sexual: coercion, assault
  • Emotional: gaslighting, threats
  • Financial: controlling money
  • Digital: GPS tracking, cyber abuse, monitoring phones and social media
The list isn’t all-inclusive.
🧩 Gaslighting, explained
Gaslighting is a form of emotional abuse in which the abuser makes the victim doubt their own memory or sanity (“That never happened; you’re imagining things”). It isolates victims because they stop trusting themselves.
💡 Exam tip
IPV isn’t only hitting: controlling money, tracking a phone by GPS, and constant threats are all IPV. Digital abuse is specifically named in the blueprint.
🚩6.15 Risk Factors for IPV & Clinical Red FlagsSlides 5–6 · Lecture
Risk categoryExamples
Slide 5 risk factorsHistory of abuse, pregnancy, substance use, isolation, low income, LGBTQ+ identity
Individual (lecture)Low self-esteem, young age (adolescents, young adults), unintended pregnancy, childhood abuse or witnessing IPV, mental health disorders, financial or emotional dependence on the partner
Partner-relatedJealousy or controlling behavior, alcohol (a huge factor) and substance use, unemployment, violent history or criminal record, belief in traditional gender roles or dominance
RelationshipConflict or dissatisfaction, unequal power dynamics, isolation
Social and culturalNorms that support aggression, lack of legal protection, limited access to education and resources, cultural acceptance of violence in relationships
🚩 Clinical red flags (slide 6 and lecture)
  • Injuries in various stages of healing; frequent injuries with vague explanations; injuries that look older than the story suggests
  • Delayed seeking of care
  • Patient hesitant to speak: fearful, anxious, withdrawn, avoids eye contact
  • Partner refuses to leave the room or insists on being present for exams; partner answers for the patient
  • Frequent missed appointments; sudden behavior changes
💡 Exam tip
If the partner won’t leave, find a way to see the patient alone (for example, “Our policy is to examine all patients privately,” or during a urine sample in the bathroom) before screening. Never ask about abuse in front of the partner.
🔄6.16 The Cycle of AbuseSlide 7 · Lecture
Phase (slide 7)What happens
1. Tension buildingStress, poor communication, fear; the victim feels like they’re “walking on eggshells”
2. IncidentPhysical, sexual, or emotional abuse occurs
3. Reconciliation (“honeymoon”)Apologies, excuses, gifts; “love bombing” (overwhelming affection and promises)
4. CalmTemporary peace; abuse may be minimized or denied. Then tension builds again
🧠 Why the cycle matters (slide 7)
  • Helps nurses recognize patterns of abuse
  • Victims may stay because of hope for change (during reconciliation and calm) or fear of escalation
⚠️ Leaving is the most dangerous time
The lecturer notes victims may try to leave 7–8 times before leaving for good, and the closer someone gets to leaving, the more violent the episodes may become. Never pressure a patient to leave; help them make a safety plan.
💡 Exam tip
A patient says, “He bought me flowers and promised it won’t happen again” → that’s the reconciliation (honeymoon) phase. Respond without judgment and keep the door open.
🔎6.17 Screening Tools, RADAR & StrangulationSlide 8 · Ch. 18 · Lecture

Screening finds IPV that patients rarely volunteer. The lecturer, an OB nurse for 26 years, has had only one patient disclose, which shows how much is missed. Ch. 18: use a validated screening tool, screen in private at annual exams, the first prenatal visit, each trimester, and the postpartum checkup (ACOG), and ask whether the woman feels safe at home and in her relationship.

🧰 Screening tools (slide 8)
  • HITS: how often does your partner Hurt, Insult, Threaten, or Scream at you?
  • Danger Assessment tool: estimates the risk of severe or lethal violence (homicide)
  • RADAR (below)
📡 RADAR (slide 8)
  • R: Routinely ask (screen everyone)
  • A: Ask in private
  • D: Document
  • A: Assess safety
  • R: Review options (resources, safety plan)
🚨 Strangulation: a lethality red flag (slide 8 and lecture)
Strangulation is obstruction of the blood vessels and airway of the neck, by hands or by objects such as cords or rope. It is one of the most lethal forms of IPV and a significant predictor of future homicide: non-fatal strangulation increases the risk of homicide by about 700%. Often there are no visible injuries (only about half have minor external marks); injuries may be neurologic or hidden. Ask about and watch for loss of consciousness, hoarseness or voice changes, tongue swelling, bleeding in the mouth, trouble swallowing or breathing, neck pain, petechiae, and memory problems. Make sure the patient gets full evaluation; some facilities have specialized strangulation examiners.
💡 Exam tip
Any report of choking or strangulation = high lethality; priority is safety assessment, medical evaluation (airway and neuro), and a safety plan, even with no marks on the neck.
🤲6.18 Trauma-Informed CareSlide 9 · Ch. 18 Clinical Judgment · Lecture

Trauma is an event or series of events experienced as physically or emotionally harmful or life-threatening, with lasting effects on functioning and well-being (SAMHSA, the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration). More than half of women experience at least one traumatic event: IPV, sexual assault, military sexual trauma, violence based on race or sexual orientation, childhood neglect, combat, disasters, community violence, refugee experiences. Trauma can cause powerlessness, fear, shame, guilt, and distrust of health care, and a nurse is often the first to notice signs.

🛡️ Principles (slide 9)
  • Assume a trauma history (it’s that common)
  • Ensure safety and trust
  • Avoid re-traumatization
  • Respect the patient’s pace
  • Ask “What happened to you?” instead of “What’s wrong with you?” (lecture)
🔁 The four Rs (Ch. 18)
  • Realize the widespread effect of trauma and paths to recovery
  • Recognize signs and symptoms of trauma
  • Respond by integrating trauma knowledge into care
  • Resist re-traumatization
Specific strategies (Ch. 18 and lecture)
  • Create a safe physical and emotional environment; be compassionate, respectful, and nonjudgmental
  • Ask permission before touching; describe each step before and during exams
  • Let clothing be shifted rather than removed when possible
  • Agree to stop the exam at any time the patient asks
  • Have the patient tell only the minimum of the story needed; after sexual assault or strangulation they’ll tell it in full to the SANE (sexual assault nurse examiner)
  • Recognize triggers in routine women’s care: pelvic exams, pregnancy, birth (especially of a daughter), postpartum care, and pelvic exams in confused older patients who may feel violated
💡 Exam tip
Trauma-informed choices give the patient control: permission, explanation, options, and the right to stop.
🤰6.19 IPV During Pregnancy & Special Populations (LGBTQ+, Elder Abuse, Legal Reporting)Slides 10–11 · Lecture
🤰 IPV during pregnancy (slide 10)
  • Increases risk for placental abruption, preterm labor, fetal demise (also miscarriage and low birth weight, slide 11)
  • Screen each trimester and postpartum (some facilities screen every visit)
  • Prioritize maternal-fetal safety
  • 1 in 6 pregnant people globally experience IPV; it often begins or escalates in pregnancy and is frequently undisclosed
  • Forms include physical violence, sexual coercion, emotional abuse, financial control, and reproductive coercion (sabotaging birth control, forcing pregnancy or abortion)
  • Lecture: homicide by a partner is a leading cause of death during pregnancy in the U.S.
👥 Special populations (slide 11)
  • LGBTQI+: higher rates because of stigma, fear of being outed, and lack of safe shelters; may face provider discrimination
  • Elder abuse: financial, physical, or emotional abuse by a caregiver or partner. Signs: malnutrition, unexplained injuries, isolation
  • Legal reporting: mandatory reporting laws vary by state; nurses must know when and how to report IPV, child, elder, or pregnant abuse
⚖️ Reporting, simplified
Child abuse and elder/dependent adult abuse are mandatory reports in every state. Reporting adult IPV depends on state law (some states require reports of certain injuries). Know your state’s rules once licensed, and tell the patient the limits of confidentiality before they disclose (6.21).
💡 Exam tip
Pregnant patient with an unexplained abdominal injury → think IPV and placental abruption: assess the fetus and the patient’s safety, and screen privately.
📱6.20 Teen & Adolescent Dating Violence and Alcohol’s Role in Sexual AssaultSlides 11–13 · Ch. 18 · Blueprint
📊 Prevalence (slides 11–12)
  • 1 in 12 U.S. high school students experience physical dating violence each year
  • 1 in 11 female and 1 in 14 male students experience sexual dating violence
🗂️ Forms (slide 12)
  • Physical: hitting, pushing, slapping
  • Emotional: jealousy, name-calling, humiliation
  • Sexual: coercion, unwanted touching
  • Digital: monitoring (checking phones, location), social media harassment, threats by text
🧠 Impacts
Mental health issues, substance use, suicidality, poor school performance.
🩺 Nursing role (slide 12)
  • Screen confidentially (see the teen alone)
  • Teach consent and healthy boundaries; healthy relationship skills prevent IPV (Ch. 18)
  • Use teen-friendly language
  • Refer: Love is Respect: call 1-866-331-9474 or text “LOVEIS” to 22522
Alcohol and sexual assault (slide 13)
  • Alcohol is the most commonly used substance in drug-facilitated sexual assault
  • It impairs judgment, motor skills, and the ability to give informed consent; perpetrators may use alcohol to exploit vulnerability
  • Alcohol does not cause sexual assault; perpetrators do. Victim intoxication never justifies assault.
  • Survivors may struggle with recovery because they can’t remember and may feel guilt about drinking; respond without blame
  • Nursing: screen sensitively in ER (emergency room) or campus settings; trauma-informed approach; provide STI, pregnancy, and forensic resources (SANE exam); refer to counseling and support services
💡 Exam tip
A teen says her boyfriend “checks my phone and tracks my location because he loves me” → digital abuse. Respond privately, teach healthy relationships, and give Love is Respect.
📝6.21 Documentation, Legal & Ethical Considerations, Referral Resources, the Nursing Role & Human TraffickingSlides 14–19 · Lecture
🖊️ Documentation guidelines (slide 14)
  1. Use patient quotes (“He pushed me into the wall”)
  2. Describe injuries objectively: size, color, location, shape
  3. Avoid assumptions (“appears to be a victim of abuse”) and loaded words like “alleged” or “claims”
  4. Use body maps and photos if allowed (with consent)
Objective, quoted documentation helps the patient most if the case goes to court.
⚖️ Legal and ethical (slide 16)
  • Know state reporting laws
  • Explain limits to confidentiality before the patient discloses
  • Always obtain informed consent (for photos, exams, reports, referrals) and help the patient understand it
📞 Referral resources (slide 15)
  • National Domestic Violence Hotline: 1-800-799-SAFE (7233)
  • Text “START” to 88788
  • Safety planning tools
  • SANE nurse (sexual assault nurse examiner); you don’t have to work in women’s health to become one
💪 Nursing role in IPV (slide 17)
  • Screen regularly
  • Provide a safe space
  • Connect to support
  • Empower survivors
Conclusion (slide 19): IPV is a public health crisis; nurses play a vital role in screening, documenting, and supporting survivors. Your presence and advocacy can save lives.
🤔 Case study (slide 18): 28-year-old pregnant patient

She avoids eye contact; her partner answers for her and refuses to leave. She has bruises on her arms and denies abuse.

  • Red flags: avoids eye contact, partner answers for her and won’t leave, arm bruises (possibly in different stages of healing), pregnancy (escalation risk), denial.
  • Nursing actions: separate the patient from the partner using policy (private exam, bathroom for a urine sample); screen privately with a validated tool; assess safety (including strangulation and weapons); assess the fetus; offer resources discreetly (hotline numbers in a safe format); safety plan; follow state reporting laws.
  • Trauma-informed response: “Many women experience problems at home. You’re not alone, and it’s not your fault. Whenever you’re ready, we can help.” Respect her pace; don’t pressure her to leave.
  • Documentation: her exact words, objective injury descriptions (size, color, location), body map or photos with consent, who was present, what resources were offered.
Human trafficking (lecture extra; good to know, not directly tested per the lecturer)

Signs often look like IPV: avoids eye contact, poor hygiene, appears coached or controlled, injuries in various stages of healing, inconsistent history, can’t speak for themselves; STIs, pregnancies, or forced abortions that don’t match the history. Higher-risk groups: minors and runaways, LGBTQ+ youth, foster care, immigrants and refugees, homeless, cognitively impaired, and people in poverty. Assess in a private, safe setting with open-ended, trauma-informed questions; screening tools include SOAR and the Trafficking Victim Identification Tool; the National Human Trafficking Hotline is 1-888-373-7888.

💡 Exam tip
Documentation questions: the correct answer uses the patient’s own words in quotes and objective measurements, never opinions.

🎮 Active Recall

Four ways to pull information out of memory instead of rereading it: flip flashcards, match terms, race the clock, or work through unfolding patient cases the way you would over a shift.

Tap a term on the left, then its match on the right. Correct pairs lock in green; wrong pairs flash red and reset.
⚡ 60-Second Speed Round
Answer as many rapid-fire questions from both modules as you can before time runs out. One point per correct answer; wrong answers just move you along.
Each case unfolds in stages. Answer each question to reveal what happens next, just like caring for a client over a shift. Cases include GIR calculations and the slide 18 IPV case.

💡 Mnemonics & Memory Aids

Every memory trick from the study sheet in one place, organized by module, for a quick review the night before.

Module 5: Neonatal Complications & Loss

🌡️ Warmth first: “Dry, Cap, Skin”

5.2 Interventions

Dry the baby, cap the head, skin-to-skin. Babies can’t shiver. Rewarm only 1–1.5 °C above their temp.

🥶 Heat loss: “Every Cold Crib Radiates”

5.2 Heat loss

Evaporation (dry the baby), Conduction (prewarm surfaces), Convection (block drafts), Radiation (away from cold walls/windows).

💉 Newborn meds: “K in the Thigh, E in the Eye”

5.21 Routine meds

Vitamin K IM in the vastus lateralis; erythromycin ointment in both eyes, both within the first hours, after warmth.

🫁 Respiratory distress: “TGRFC”

5.1 Assessment

Tachypnea (over 60), Grunting, Retractions, Flaring, Cyanosis.

🐣 Preemie priorities: “Breathe, Bake, Feed, Protect”

5.3 Preterm

Breathing → warmth → glucose/feeding → infection prevention, plus family.

🫧 RDS: “Soap is missing”

5.4 RDS

Surfactant works like soap to keep alveoli open; replace it via the ET tube + CPAP.

☁️ Too much O₂ hurts “Lungs and Lenses”

5.5 BPD/ROP

Oxygen toxicity: BPD (lungs) and ROP (retina). Keep SpO₂ in range.

🔄 “Indo closes, PGE opens”

5.5 / 5.14 Ductus

Indomethacin/ibuprofen close a PDA; prostaglandin E1 keeps the ductus open for heart defects.

💚 MAS: “Late, Green, Barrel”

5.6 MAS

Post-term, green fluid, barrel chest with coarse crackles. Watch PPHN and pneumothorax.

🍬 Hypoglycemia: “Small stores or big insulin”

5.7–5.8

SGA = small stores; IDM = too much insulin. Both drop glucose.

🧮 GIR: “% times rate over 6 times kilo”

5.8 GIR

GIR = (% × mL/hr) ÷ (6 × kg). Target 5–8 mg/kg/min.

💛 Jaundice: “Day one is done wrong”

5.9 Jaundice

Jaundice in the first 24 hours = pathologic. Physiologic appears after 24 hours.

😎 Phototherapy: “Shades, Diaper, Flip, Feed”

5.9 Phototherapy

Eye shields, diaper only, turn often, feed every 2–3 hours.

🫧 NAS: “WITHDRAWAL”

5.10 NAS

Wakefulness, Irritability, Tremors, Hyperreflexia, Diarrhea, Respiratory rate up, Autonomic (sweat, yawn), Weight loss, Alert high-pitched cry, Lots of sneezing.

🤱 ESC: “Eat, Sleep, Console”

5.10 NAS

Can the baby eat, sleep an hour, and be consoled within 10–20 minutes?

🫃 NEC: “Belly Big, Bloody, Back-up”

5.11 NEC

Distention, bloody stools, rising residuals → hold feeds, decompress.

🧠 IVH: “Midline, Minimal, Slow”

5.12 IVH

Midline head, minimal handling, slow fluids.

🦠 Sepsis: “Culture before cure”

5.13 Sepsis

Draw cultures, then ampicillin + gentamicin immediately.

🚗 Discharge: “Seat, Screens, CPR”

5.15 Discharge

Car seat challenge, all screens done, infant CPR and equipment teaching.

📟 Monitor alarm: “Baby before box”

5.15 Apnea monitor

Check the baby first, not the monitor.

🕊️ Loss cutoffs: “20 still, 28 neo”

5.16 Types

Stillbirth at 20+ weeks; neonatal death under 28 days.

💬 Grief talk: “Name, Feel, Share”

5.19 Communication

Use the baby’s name, validate the feeling, invite them to share. No clichés.

Module 6: Women’s Health & IPV

❤️ Women’s MI: “Jaw, Back, Tired, Nauseous”

6.2 CVD

Women often present with jaw/back pain, fatigue, nausea, cold sweats.

🌱 Puberty: “Breasts, Hair, Period”

6.3 Puberty

Thelarche → adrenarche → menarche.

🔢 Lifestyle numbers: “150, 1, 15, 30”

6.4 Lifestyle

150 min/week exercise, 1 drink/day, SPF 15+, BMI 30 = obesity.

🔥 Menopause: “12 months, ↓ estrogen, hot flash”

6.5 Menopause

Menopause = 12 months without a period; key symptom hot flashes.

🧊 Hot flash relief: “Cool, Layer, Avoid”

6.6 Management

Cool room, dress in layers, avoid alcohol, caffeine, spicy food, heat.

🛡️ “Uterus? Add progesterone”

6.6 HRT

Estrogen alone with a uterus raises endometrial cancer risk; question the order.

🚫 Estrogen contraindications: “Bleeding, Blood clots, Breast, Big BP, Bile”

6.6 HRT

Unexplained bleeding, clots/PE, breast or uterine cancer, untreated hypertension, liver/gallbladder disease.

🎂 Screening birthdays: “21, 35, 40, 45, 50, 65”

6.8 Screenings

Cervical 21 · diabetes 35 if overweight · mammogram/eye 40 · colorectal 45 · Shingrix 50 · DXA/pneumococcal 65.

🦴 T-score: “Minus two and a half, bones are in half”

6.9 Osteoporosis

−2.5 or lower = osteoporosis; −1 to −2.5 = osteopenia.

💧 Fosamax: “Water, Wait, Walk tall”

6.9 Alendronate

8 oz water, wait 30 minutes to eat, stay upright 30 minutes.

🏠 Fall-proof: “Rugs out, Rails in, Rise slow”

6.10 Older women

Remove rugs, grab bars, rise slowly, nonskid shoes, yearly eye exam.

📚 Barriers: “Rural = Remote, Language = Interpreter, Literacy = Teach-back”

6.12 SDOH

Telehealth/mobile clinics, professional interpreters, teach-back.

🪞 Humility: “You’re the expert”

6.13 LGBTQ+

Cultural humility vs. competence (“I’m the expert”).

🗂️ IPV forms: “PSEFD” (Please Stop Every Form of Damage)

6.14 Forms

Physical, Sexual, Emotional, Financial, Digital.

🔄 Cycle: “Tension, Incident, Reconcile, Calm” (TIRC)

6.16 Cycle

Apologies and gifts = reconciliation.

📡 RADAR

6.17 Screening

Routinely ask, Ask in private, Document, Assess safety, Review options.

🚨 “No marks ≠ no danger”

6.17 Strangulation

Strangulation raises homicide risk about 700%, often with no visible injury.

🤲 Trauma-informed: “Permission, Explain, Stop”

6.18 TIC

Ask before touching, describe every step, stop when asked. “What happened to you?”

📱 Teens: “Love is Respect, text LOVEIS”

6.20 Teens

1-866-331-9474 or text LOVEIS to 22522.

🖊️ Documentation: “Quote it, Measure it, Don’t judge it”

6.21 Documentation

Patient quotes, objective sizes and colors, no assumptions or “alleged.”

💪 Nursing role: “Screen, Provide, Connect, Empower” (SPCE)

6.21 Nursing role

Screen regularly, provide a safe space, connect to support, empower survivors.
